# ouija 0.1.0-alpha.209 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ouija/0.1.0-alpha.209

# ouija

*A transparent pipe between coding sessions through tmux.*

You're deep in a coding session when you realize another session has the understanding you need. Maybe it started on something unrelated on your machine, maybe it's on your laptop at home. You say "ask deploy-infra what port the gateway uses." The other session receives it as natural input, draws on what it knows, and replies. Every session stays fully interactive for you.

Ad hoc by design. Sessions don't need to be started any special way. Run ouija, open coding sessions as you normally would, and they discover each other. For same-machine messaging that's all you need. For cross-machine, pair two ouija daemons once over Nostr and any session on either machine becomes reachable.

ouija is plumbing, not a harness. It delivers messages between sessions and manages their lifecycle. The protocol is open, the transport is end-to-end encrypted, and sessions keep their own memory, tools, and context. Today ouija supports Claude Code (primary, well-tested) and opencode (integrated, less battle-tested). Additional backends would plug in through the same hook and API surface the existing ones use.

The session lifecycle primitives (spawn, kill, health checks, worktree isolation) may also be useful beneath a higher-level harness or orchestrator, but ouija itself stays small: discover sessions, deliver messages, and keep sessions reachable.

## Prerequisites

[tmux](https://github.com/tmux/tmux) and at least one supported coding assistant: [Claude Code](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code) or [opencode](https://opencode.ai).

## Quick start

```
```
If a matching prebuilt release artifact is available for your platform, `cargo binstall ouija` can install it without compiling.

`ouija start-server` runs the daemon in the foreground. Keep it running in that terminal, or run it under your service manager.

The daemon auto-configures your coding assistant (hooks, skills). In another terminal, open a session inside tmux:

` && `Sessions auto-register using the working directory name (e.g. `/code/api` becomes `api`). Start talking:

"Use ouija to ask deploy what port the gateway is exposed on"

## What you can do

**Message any session**, local or remote. Sessions discover each other automatically. Messages travel through a short CLI command (`ouija ask target "question"`) instead of making the assistant compose raw HTTP requests.

**Share state through the filesystem, not just the wire.** A message can be small and point to shared state: "see `docs/api.md`" or "check the worktree at `~/code/foo`". The receiver loads the full content from disk, bypassing the compression that any fixed-size message would impose. Messages as pointers to shared state scale better than messages as state.

**Spawn sessions on the fly.** Ask the assistant to start a new session (e.g. "use ouija to start a gateway-debug session"). The daemon creates a tmux window, launches a coding session, and registers it. You can specify a prompt to seed the session with context and a backend (`claude-code` or `opencode`).

**Long-running work.** Two mechanisms for recurring work:

- **Loops**-- the session drives itself. Simple — the session's prompt and reminder tell it what to do and how to signal completion. The daemon handles the restart cycle.
- **Tasks**(cron) -- the daemon drives the session. Good for periodic checks, daily reports, scheduled maintenance. If the target session is dead, the daemon revives it with the task's prompt + reminder.

**Peer-to-peer collaboration.** No hierarchy. Two long-running sessions can message each other directly — one optimizing a skill while the other evaluates results, or one migrating files while the other reviews the diffs. They coordinate through the ouija skill's send capability, not through a central orchestrator.

**Always interactive.** Every session runs in a tmux pane. You can jump into any session at any time — watch it work, type a correction, answer a question, or take over. The session doesn't know or care whether the next input comes from a peer session or from you at the keyboard.

**Worktree sessions.** Spawn sessions in isolated git worktrees for parallel work on the same repo without branch conflicts.

**Nostr DMs.** If you use Nostr, configure your npub to control the daemon from any Nostr client. Send `/list`, `/start`, `@session message`, or bare text (routed by an LLM).

**Dashboard** at `http://localhost:7880`. Manage sessions, tasks, node connections, and settings.

## Design philosophy

**ouija is transport, not intelligence.** Sessions compose their own messages, interpret what they receive, and decide what to do. ouija delivers bytes. That is deliberate.

**Messages are compression.** When a session sends a message, it is compressing its current understanding into a few hundred tokens. The transport is lossless but the composition is lossy. For anything larger than a paragraph, prefer pointing at shared state (a file, a wiki page, a worktree) rather than dumping context into the message body.

**Receiving sessions can drop information.** Even when a message arrives intact, the receiver may fail to integrate it with its existing context. This is a property of LLMs, not ouija. Treat inter-session messaging as persuasion, not injection: explicit, cited, and verifiable against shared artifacts.

**Stale claims transfer invisibly.** If session A tells session B "the database is sharded by tenant," and A's mental model is actually outdated, B will treat the claim as fact. Prefer pointers to ground truth over assertions whenever it matters.

## Connecting machines

On machine A:

```
```
On machine B:

```
```
Sessions on both machines discover each other. Tickets contain a connect secret, only authorized nodes can communicate. After connecting, both nodes remember each other and auto-reconnect on restart.

## Message protocol

Sessions communicate through XML messages delivered to the coding assistant:

```
what port does the gateway use?
```
Messages can reference earlier ones for conversation threading:

- `re="47"`— progress update on task 47
- `re="47" done="true"`— task 47 is complete

The daemon assigns unique IDs to every message, tracks pending replies, and nudges sessions that haven't responded. Sessions interact via the `ouija` CLI and the ouija skill -- the XML is handled automatically.

## How it works

- Each machine runs an **ouija daemon**(small Rust binary)
- Sessions **auto-register via hooks**on startup
- Local messages: **tmux injection**(Claude Code) or**HTTP API**(opencode)
- Remote messages: **end-to-end encrypted**over[Nostr](https://nostr.com)relays. No central server, no direct TCP connection required, works across NATs, and relays see only ciphertext. Unusual for agent communication, since most frameworks assume a reachable IP or a proprietary cloud.
- Node auth: **connect secret**in the ticket, unknown senders rejected

All session state transitions go through a pure state machine (`DaemonProtocol`) with a [Stateright](https://github.com/stateright/stateright) model check in [ daemon_protocol.rs](https://docs.rs/src/daemon_protocol.rs).

## Security

- **Tickets are secrets.**Share out-of-band only (copy/paste, not through the assistant).
- **Connect secret auth.**Unknown senders are rejected.
- **Encrypted transport.**End-to-end encrypted via Nostr (- [NIP-17](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/17.md)gift-wrapped DMs). Relays cannot read content.
- **Localhost only.**The daemon binds to- `127.0.0.1`.
- **Keep tickets out of chats.**Normal session APIs do not expose tickets, but any assistant with shell access can run CLI commands you ask it to run.
- **Persistent logs are metadata-only.**- `messages.jsonl`records routing metadata; the dashboard may show recent in-memory message content until restart.

### Claude Code permissions

Ouija does not force Claude Code into bypass-permissions mode by default. Spawned Claude sessions inherit your Claude Code settings, such as `permissions.defaultMode` in `~/.claude/settings.json`.

If you run ouija inside an isolated environment and want spawned Claude sessions to skip permission prompts, opt in explicitly:

## CLI

Outside tmux, such as an OpenCode HTTP/API tool process, pass the public registered Ouija session id as the sender: `ouija ask <to> "msg" --from <public-ouija-id>`. Do not use backend labels like `opencode` or opaque OpenCode `backend_session_id` values as `--from`.

Run `ouija --help` for the full command list.

## Data

Config in `~/.config/ouija/` (settings, identity). Data in `~/.local/share/ouija/` (sessions, tasks, connections). Persistent message logs are metadata-only.

## Tmux integration

Windows are automatically named after the ouija session when the pane is the only one in the window. Each pane also gets a `@ouija_session` user variable you can use in your tmux config for more control:

```
set -g window-status-current-format '#{?@ouija_session,⊕ #{@ouija_session},#{b:pane_current_path}}'
```
Fuzzy session pickers that read tmux's display format will show ouija session names automatically. The author uses [dcadenas/tmux-sessionizer](https://github.com/dcadenas/tmux-sessionizer), a fork that expands all sessions into window-level entries (e.g. `ouija/1:⊕ daily-report`), making ouija sessions easy to find and switch to.

## Testing

# voprf_vx - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/voprf-vx/1.0.0-rc.0/voprf_vx/

## Expand description

An implementation of a verifiable oblivious pseudorandom function (VOPRF)

Note: This implementation is in sync with
[RFC 9497](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497).

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

A verifiable oblivious pseudorandom function is a protocol that is evaluated between a client and a server. They must first agree on a finite cyclic group along with a point representation.

We will use the following choice in this example:

[§](https://docs.rs#modes-of-operation)Modes of Operation

VOPRF can be used in three modes:

- [Base Mode](https://docs.rs#base-mode), which corresponds to a normal OPRF evaluation with no support for the verification of the OPRF outputs
- [Verifiable Mode](https://docs.rs#verifiable-mode), which corresponds to an OPRF evaluation where the outputs can be verified against a server public key (VOPRF)
- [Partially Oblivious Verifiable Mode](https://docs.rs#metadata), which corresponds to a VOPRF, where a public input can be supplied to the PRF computation

In all of these modes, the protocol begins with a client blinding, followed by a server evaluation, and finishes with a client finalization and server evaluation.

[§](https://docs.rs#base-mode)Base Mode

In base mode, an [OprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html) interacts with an [OprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html) to compute the
output of the OPRF.

[§](https://docs.rs#server-setup)Server Setup

The protocol begins with a setup phase, in which the server must run
[OprfServer::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.new) to produce an instance of itself. This instance must be
persisted on the server and used for online client evaluations.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::OprfServer;
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let server = OprfServer::<CipherSuite>::new(&mut server_rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#client-blinding)Client Blinding

In the first step, the client chooses an input, and runs [OprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html#method.blind)
to produce an [OprfClientBlindResult](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClientBlindResult.html), which consists of a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html)
to be sent to the server and an [OprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html) which must be persisted on the
client for the final step of the VOPRF protocol.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::OprfClient;
let mut client_rng = SysRng;
let client_blind_result = OprfClient::<CipherSuite>::blind(b"input", &mut client_rng)
    .expect("Unable to construct client");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-blind-evaluation)Server Blind Evaluation

In the second step, the server takes as input the message from
[OprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html#method.blind) (a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html)), and runs
[OprfServer::blind_evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.blind_evaluate) to produce [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html) to be sent to
the client.

`let server_evaluate_result = server.blind_evaluate(&client_blind_result.message);`[§](https://docs.rs#client-finalization)Client Finalization

In the final step on the client side, the client takes as input the message
from [OprfServer::evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.evaluate) (an [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html)), and runs
[OprfClient::finalize](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html#method.finalize) to produce an output for the protocol.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(b"input", &message)
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
println!("VOPRF output: {:?}", client_finalize_result.to_vec());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-evaluation)Server Evaluation

Optionally, if the server has direct access to the PRF input, then it need
not perform the oblivious computation and can simply run
[OprfServer::evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.evaluate) to generate an output which matches the output
produced by an execution of the oblivious protocol on the same input and
key.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(b"input", &message)
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
let server_evaluate_result = server
    .evaluate(b"input")
    .expect("Unable to perform the server evaluation");
assert_eq!(client_finalize_result, server_evaluate_result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#verifiable-mode)Verifiable Mode

In verifiable mode, a [VoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html) interacts with a [VoprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html) to
compute the output of the VOPRF. In order to verify the server’s
computation, the client checks a server-generated proof against the server’s
public key. If the proof fails to verify, then the client does not receive
an output.

In batch mode, a single proof can be used for multiple VOPRF evaluations.
See [the batching section](https://docs.rs#batching) for more details on how to perform
batch evaluations.

[§](https://docs.rs#server-setup-1)Server Setup

The protocol begins with a setup phase, in which the server must run
[VoprfServer::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.new) to produce an instance of itself. This instance must be
persisted on the server and used for online client evaluations.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::VoprfServer;
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let server = VoprfServer::<CipherSuite>::new(&mut server_rng).unwrap();
// To be sent to the client
println!("Server public key: {:?}", server.get_public_key());
```
The public key should be sent to the client, since the client will need it in the final step of the protocol in order to complete the evaluation of the VOPRF.

[§](https://docs.rs#client-blinding-1)Client Blinding

In the first step, the client chooses an input, and runs
[VoprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.blind) to produce a [VoprfClientBlindResult](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClientBlindResult.html), which consists
of a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html) to be sent to the server and a [VoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html) which
must be persisted on the client for the final step of the VOPRF protocol.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::VoprfClient;
let mut client_rng = SysRng;
let client_blind_result = VoprfClient::<CipherSuite>::blind(b"input", &mut client_rng)
    .expect("Unable to construct client");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-blind-evaluation-1)Server Blind Evaluation

In the second step, the server takes as input the message from
[VoprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.blind) (a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html)), and runs
[VoprfServer::blind_evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.blind_evaluate) to produce a [VoprfServerEvaluateResult](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServerEvaluateResult.html),
which consists of an [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html) to be sent to the client along with
a proof.

```
let VoprfServerEvaluateResult { message, proof } =
    server.blind_evaluate(&mut server_rng, &client_blind_result.message);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#client-finalization-1)Client Finalization

In the final step, the client takes as input the message from
[VoprfServer::blind_evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.blind_evaluate) (an [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html)), the proof, and the
server’s public key, and runs [VoprfClient::finalize](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.finalize) to produce an output
for the protocol.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(
        b"input",
        &server_evaluate_result.message,
        &server_evaluate_result.proof,
        server.get_public_key(),
    )
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
println!("VOPRF output: {:?}", client_finalize_result.to_vec());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-evaluation-1)Server Evaluation

Optionally, if the server has direct access to the PRF input, then it need
not perform the oblivious computation and can simply run
[VoprfServer::evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.evaluate) to generate an output which matches the output
produced by an execution of the oblivious protocol on the same input and
key.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(
        b"input",
        &server_evaluate_result.message,
        &server_evaluate_result.proof,
        server.get_public_key(),
    )
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
let server_evaluate_result = server
    .evaluate(b"input")
    .expect("Unable to perform the server evaluation");
assert_eq!(client_finalize_result, server_evaluate_result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-usage)Advanced Usage

There are two additional (and optional) extensions to the core VOPRF protocol: support for batching of evaluations, and support for public metadata.

[§](https://docs.rs#batching)Batching

It is sometimes desirable to generate only a single, constant-size proof for
an unbounded number of VOPRF evaluations (on arbitrary inputs).
[VoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html) and [VoprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html) support a batch API for handling this case.
In the following example, we show how to use the batch API to produce a
single proof for 10 parallel VOPRF evaluations.

First, the client produces 10 blindings, storing their resulting states and messages:

```
let mut client_rng = SysRng;
let mut client_states = vec![];
let mut client_messages = vec![];
for _ in 0..10 {
    let client_blind_result = VoprfClient::<CipherSuite>::blind(b"input", &mut client_rng)
        .expect("Unable to construct client");
    client_states.push(client_blind_result.state);
    client_messages.push(client_blind_result.message);
}
```
Next, the server calls the [VoprfServer::batch_blind_evaluate_prepare](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.batch_blind_evaluate_prepare) and
[VoprfServer::batch_blind_evaluate_finish](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.batch_blind_evaluate_finish) function on a set of client
messages, to produce a corresponding set of messages to be returned to the
client (returned in the same order), along with a single proof:

```
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let prepared_evaluation_elements = server.batch_blind_evaluate_prepare(client_messages.iter());
let prepared_elements: Vec<_> = prepared_evaluation_elements.collect();
let VoprfServerBatchEvaluateFinishResult { messages, proof } = server
    .batch_blind_evaluate_finish(&mut server_rng, client_messages.iter(), &prepared_elements)
    .expect("Unable to perform server batch evaluate");
let messages: Vec<_> = messages.collect();
```
If `alloc` is available, `VoprfServer::batch_blind_evaluate` can be called
to avoid having to collect output manually:

```
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let VoprfServerBatchEvaluateResult { messages, proof } = server
    .batch_blind_evaluate(&mut server_rng, &client_messages)
    .expect("Unable to perform server batch evaluate");
```
Then, the client calls [VoprfClient::batch_finalize](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.batch_finalize) on the client states
saved from the first step, along with the messages returned by the server,
along with the server’s proof, in order to produce a vector of outputs if
the proof verifies correctly.

```
let client_batch_finalize_result = VoprfClient::batch_finalize(
    &[b"input"; 10],
    &client_states,
    &messages,
    &proof,
    server.get_public_key(),
)
.expect("Unable to perform client batch finalization")
.collect::<Vec<_>>();
println!("VOPRF batch outputs: {:?}", client_batch_finalize_result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#metadata)Metadata

The optional metadata parameter included in the POPRF mode allows clients and servers to cryptographically bind additional data to the VOPRF output. This metadata is known to both parties at the start of the protocol, and is inserted under the server’s blind evaluate step and the client’s finalize step. This metadata can be constructed with some type of higher-level domain separation to avoid cross-protocol attacks or related issues.

The API for POPRF mode is similar to VOPRF mode, except that a [PoprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.PoprfServer.html)
and [PoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.PoprfClient.html) are used, and that each of the functions accept an
additional (and optional) info parameter which represents the public input.
See
[https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497#name-poprf-public-input](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497#name-poprf-public-input)
for more detailed information on how this public input should be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

-
The `alloc`feature requires Rust’s`alloc`crate and enables batching VOPRF evaluations.
-
The `serde`feature, enabled by default, provides convenience functions for serializing and deserializing with[serde](https://serde.rs/).
-
The `danger`feature, disabled by default, exposes functions for setting and getting internal values not available in the default API. These functions are intended for use in by higher-level cryptographic protocols that need access to these raw values and are able to perform the necessary validations on them (such as being valid group elements).
-
The `ristretto255-ciphersuite`features enables using`Ristretto255``CipherSuite`
-
The `ristretto255`feature enables using`Ristretto255`[Group](https://docs.rs/trait.Group.html)choice. To select a specific backend see the[curve25519-dalek](https://docs.rs/(https:/docs.rs/curve25519-dalek/4.0.0-pre.5/curve25519_dalek/index.html#backends))documentation.

# rmcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rmcp/2.1.0/rmcp/

## Expand description

The official Rust SDK for the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25). Build MCP servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts to AI assistants — or build clients that connect to them.

For **getting started**, **usage guides**, and **full MCP feature documentation** (resources, prompts, sampling, roots, logging, completions, subscriptions, etc.), see the [main README](https://docs.rs/README.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

| Feature | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | Server functionality and the tool system | ✅ |
| `client` | Client functionality | |
| `macros` | `#[tool]`/`#[prompt]`macros (re-exports)`rmcp-macros` | ✅ |
| `schemars` | JSON Schema generation for tool definitions | |
| `auth` | OAuth 2.0 authentication support | |
| `elicitation` | Elicitation support |

[§](https://docs.rs#transport-features)Transport features

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `transport-io` | Server-side stdio transport |
| `transport-child-process` | Client-side stdio transport (spawns a child process) |
| `transport-async-rw` | Generic async read/write transport |
| `transport-streamable-http-client` | Streamable HTTP client (transport-agnostic) |
| `transport-streamable-http-client-reqwest` | Streamable HTTP client with default `reqwest`backend |
| `transport-streamable-http-server` | Streamable HTTP server transport |

[§](https://docs.rs#tls-backend-options-for-http-transports)TLS backend options (for HTTP transports)

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `reqwest` | Uses rustls — pure Rust TLS (recommended default) |
| `reqwest-native-tls` | Uses platform-native TLS (OpenSSL / Secure Transport / SChannel) |
| `reqwest-tls-no-provider` | Uses rustls without a default crypto provider (bring your own) |

[§](https://docs.rs#transports)Transports

The transport layer is pluggable. Two built-in pairs cover the most common cases:

| Client | Server | |
|---|---|---|
| stdio | `TokioChildProcess` | `stdio` |
| Streamable HTTP | `StreamableHttpClientTransport` | `StreamableHttpService` |

Any type that implements the [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) trait can be used. The

[helper trait provides automatic conversions from:](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.IntoTransport.html)

`IntoTransport`- `(Sink, Stream)`or a combined- `Sink + Stream`
- `(AsyncRead, AsyncWrite)`or a combined- `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`
- A `Worker`
- A `Transport`

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This project is licensed under the terms specified in the repository’s [LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE) file.

# ferridriver_expect - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver-expect/0.5.0/ferridriver_expect/

## Expand description

Value matchers (Jest-compatible) and asymmetric matchers for
ferridriver’s `expect()` API. Shared between the test runner
(`ferridriver-test`) and the QuickJS scripting layer
(`ferridriver-script`) so both surfaces dispatch through the same
Rust core (per [the Rust-is-the-source-of-truth rule](https://github.com/salamaashoush/ferridriver/blob/main/CLAUDE.md)).

Web-first matchers (locator/page/apiResponse) still live in
`ferridriver-test::expect` because they need the test runner’s
polling + screenshot context. This crate is intentionally tiny:
`regex`, `serde`, `serde_json` deps only.

- `pub use value::`- [expect_value](https://docs.rs/value/fn.expect_value.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [api_](https://docs.rs/api_response/index.html)- response
- `expect(apiResponse).toBeOK()`— synchronous status check on a captured- `ferridriver::http_client::HttpResponse`.
- [asymmetric](https://docs.rs/asymmetric/index.html)
- Asymmetric matchers (`expect.any`,`expect.objectContaining`, …). Wire-encoded as a tagged JSON object so the script layer can produce them in JS and have them round-trip through`serde_json::Value`.
- [builder](https://docs.rs/builder/index.html)
- `Expect<T>`builder shared by every consumer (test runner, QuickJS binding, plain Rust callers). Targets are subjects of web-first matchers —- `&Locator`,- `&Arc<Page>`,- `&HttpResponse`. Value matchers live on- `crate::ExpectValue`
- [diff](https://docs.rs/diff/index.html)
- Unified-diff rendering for assertion failures.
- [locator](https://docs.rs/locator/index.html)
- Locator web-first matchers — single source of truth shared by the
test runner (`ferridriver-test`) and the QuickJS binding (`ferridriver-script`). Screenshot / aria-snapshot / value-snapshot matchers stay in`ferridriver-test`because they pull in image and aria-YAML infrastructure that does not belong in this lightweight crate.
- [page](https://docs.rs/page/index.html)
- Page web-first matchers — url + title only. Snapshot/screenshot/
aria matchers live in `ferridriver-test`because they need the test-runner’s snapshot directory + image pipeline.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/poll/index.html)
- Generic async polling primitives shared by the test runner’s
`Expect<T>`and the script-layer`ExpectJs`binding.
- [throw](https://docs.rs/throw/index.html)
- Synchronous `toThrow`matcher (Jest’s`expect(fn).toThrow(...)`).
- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)
- Synchronous value matchers (Jest-style).

# rmcp_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rmcp-macros/2.1.0/rmcp_macros/

## Expand description

Procedural macros for the [RMCP](https://docs.rs/rmcp) SDK. Most users should depend on `rmcp` with the `macros` feature (enabled by default) rather than using this crate directly.

For **getting started** and **full MCP feature documentation**, see the [main README](https://docs.rs/README.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#available-macros)Available Macros

| Macro | Description |
|---|---|
| `#[tool]` | Mark a function as an MCP tool handler |
| `#[tool_router]` | Generate a tool router from an impl block (optional `server_handler`flag elides a separate`#[tool_handler]`block for tools-only servers) |
| `#[tool_handler]` | Generate `call_tool`and`list_tools`handler methods |
| `#[prompt]` | Mark a function as an MCP prompt handler |
| `#[prompt_router]` | Generate a prompt router from an impl block |
| `#[prompt_handler]` | Generate `get_prompt`and`list_prompts`handler methods |
| `#[task_handler]` | Wire up the task lifecycle on top of an `OperationProcessor` |

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-example)Quick Example

Tools-only server with a single `impl` block (`server_handler` expands `#[tool_handler]` in a second macro pass):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use rmcp::{tool, tool_router};
#[derive(Clone)]
struct MyServer;
#[tool_router(server_handler)]
impl MyServer {
    #[tool(description = "Say hello")]
    async fn hello(&self) -> String {
        "Hello, world!".into()
    }
}
```
If you need custom `#[tool_handler(...)]` arguments (e.g. `instructions`, `name`, or stacked `#[prompt_handler]` on the same `impl ServerHandler`), use two blocks instead:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use rmcp::{tool, tool_router, tool_handler, ServerHandler};
#[derive(Clone)]
struct MyServer;
#[tool_router]
impl MyServer {
    #[tool(description = "Say hello")]
    async fn hello(&self) -> String {
        "Hello, world!".into()
    }
}
#[tool_handler]
impl ServerHandler for MyServer {}
```
See the [full documentation](https://docs.rs/rmcp-macros) for detailed usage of each macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This project is licensed under the terms specified in the repository’s [LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE) file.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [prompt](https://docs.rs/attr.prompt.html)
- prompt
- [prompt_](https://docs.rs/attr.prompt_handler.html)- handler
- prompt_handler
- [prompt_](https://docs.rs/attr.prompt_router.html)- router
- prompt_router
- [task_](https://docs.rs/attr.task_handler.html)- handler
- task_handler

- tool

# sidereon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon/0.10.1/sidereon/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sidereon)sidereon

A thin, ergonomic API over the [ sidereon_core](https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.10.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sidereon_core/index.html) engine. It does not model
anything itself: every function here delegates to a

`sidereon_core` reference
entry point and re-exports its result structs, so the numerical behavior is
identical to calling the core directly. The value it adds is a small, human
surface:- `load_sp3`
- `parse_antex`- `load_antex`
- `parse_rinex_nav`- `load_rinex_nav`
- `parse_rinex_obs`- `load_rinex_obs`
- `parse_rinex_clock`- `load_rinex_clock`
- `decode_crinex`- `load_crinex`
- `solve_spp`
- `solve_velocity`
- `solve_rtk_float_with`- `solve_rtk_fixed_with`
- `solve_ppp_float_with`- `solve_ppp_fixed_with`
- GNSS utility modules such as `frequencies``combinations``quality``carrier_phase``signal``velocity``broadcast_comparison``constants``navigation``geometry``data``dgnss``constellation``ppp_corrections``rtk``staleness``tides``ils``terrain`
- `astro`
- `tle`- `sgp4`- `passes`- `tca`
- one `Error`

The input, result, and ephemeris types each function takes and returns are
re-exported from `sidereon_core` under [ antex](https://docs.rs/antex/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/rinex/index.html)

`rinex`[,](https://docs.rs/astro/index.html)

`astro`[,](https://docs.rs/ephemeris/index.html)

`ephemeris`[,](https://docs.rs/positioning/index.html)

`positioning`[, and the curated](https://docs.rs/observables/index.html)

`observables`[/](https://docs.rs/rtk_filter/index.html)

`rtk_filter`[facades, so a consumer imports the ergonomic API types from this one crate. Lower-level RTK/PPP internals remain available under](https://docs.rs/precise_positioning/index.html)

`precise_positioning`[with their native core errors.](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html)

`raw````
// Malformed input surfaces a single error type.
let parsed = sidereon::load_sp3(b"not a valid sp3 file");
assert!(matches!(parsed, Err(sidereon::Error::Sp3(_))));
```
Lower-level helpers re-exported through modules such as [ rinex](https://docs.rs/rinex/index.html) keep their
native core error type. Map them explicitly at wrapper boundaries; there is
intentionally no blanket conversion into

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)

`Error`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn decode_from_reexported_core() -> sidereon::Result<()> {
    sidereon::rinex::decode_crinex("not a CRINEX file\n")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
Low-level RTK and PPP core modules live behind the explicit [ raw](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html) escape
hatch, not the ergonomic facades.

`let _ = sidereon::raw::rtk_filter::RtkFilterScratch::new();`Hot-path RTK filter APIs are intentionally not part of the ergonomic
`sidereon::rtk_filter` facade.

PPP preparation and raw solver APIs are intentionally not part of the
ergonomic `sidereon::precise_positioning` facade.

RTK config builders consume the config. Dropping the returned value must not leave an unchanged copy available for solving.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use sidereon::{
    rtk_filter::{FloatSolveOpts, MeasModel, StochasticModel},
    RtkFloatConfig,
};
let epochs = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_ids = Vec::<String>::new();
let model = MeasModel {
    code_sigma_m: 0.3,
    phase_sigma_m: 0.003,
    sagnac: true,
    stochastic: StochasticModel::Rtklib,
};
let opts = FloatSolveOpts {
    position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
    ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
    max_iterations: 1,
};
let config = RtkFloatConfig::new(&epochs, [0.0; 3], &ambiguity_ids, &model, opts);
config.with_initial_baseline_m([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]);
let _ = sidereon::solve_rtk_float_with(config);
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use sidereon::{
    rtk_filter::{
        AmbiguityScale, AmbiguitySet, FixedSolveOpts, FloatSolveOpts, MeasModel,
        ResidualValidationOpts, StochasticModel, ValidatedFixedSolveOpts,
    },
    RtkFixedConfig,
};
let epochs = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_ids = Vec::<String>::new();
let ambiguity_satellites = BTreeMap::new();
let wavelengths_m = BTreeMap::new();
let offsets_m = BTreeMap::new();
let float_only_systems = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_set = AmbiguitySet {
    ids: &ambiguity_ids,
    satellites: &ambiguity_satellites,
    scale: AmbiguityScale {
        wavelengths_m: &wavelengths_m,
        offsets_m: &offsets_m,
    },
    float_only_systems: &float_only_systems,
};
let model = MeasModel {
    code_sigma_m: 0.3,
    phase_sigma_m: 0.003,
    sagnac: true,
    stochastic: StochasticModel::Rtklib,
};
let opts = ValidatedFixedSolveOpts {
    float: FloatSolveOpts {
        position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        max_iterations: 1,
    },
    fixed: FixedSolveOpts {
        position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        max_iterations: 1,
        ratio_threshold: 3.0,
        partial_ambiguity_resolution: false,
        partial_min_ambiguities: 4,
    },
    residual: ResidualValidationOpts {
        threshold_sigma: None,
        max_exclusions: 0,
    },
};
let config = RtkFixedConfig::new(&epochs, [0.0; 3], ambiguity_set, &model, opts);
config.with_initial_baseline_m([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]);
let _ = sidereon::solve_rtk_fixed_with(config);
```

## Expand description

Common plugin descriptors, state, and graph adapters.

```
use sim_lib_plugin_core::{
    ParameterDescriptor, PluginDescriptor, PluginFormat, PluginState,
};
let descriptor = PluginDescriptor::audio_effect(
    PluginFormat::Sim,
    "org.sim.doc-gain",
    "Doc Gain",
    2,
)
.unwrap()
.with_parameter(ParameterDescriptor::new(0, "gain", "Gain", 0.0, 2.0, 1.0).unwrap());
assert_eq!(descriptor.parameter(0).unwrap().plain_to_normalized(1.0), 0.5);
let mut state = PluginState::new();
state.set_param(0, 1.0);
let rebuilt = PluginState::from_expr(&state.to_expr()).unwrap();

```

# once_cell 1.21.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/once_cell/1.21.4

# Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, `unsync::OnceCell` and `sync::OnceCell`. `OnceCell`
might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can be assigned to at most once and provide direct access
to the stored contents. In a nutshell, API looks *roughly* like this:

```
```
Note that, like with `RefCell` and `Mutex`, the `set` method requires only a shared reference.
Because of the single assignment restriction `get` can return an `&T` instead of `Ref<T>`
or `MutexGuard<T>`.

`once_cell` also has a `Lazy<T>` type, build on top of `OnceCell` which provides the same API as
the `lazy_static!` macro, but without using any macros:

```
use ;
use Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA:  = new;
```
More patterns and use-cases are in the [docs](https://docs.rs/once_cell/)!

# once_cell - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/once_cell/1.21.4/target-redirect/once_cell/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, [ unsync::OnceCell](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.OnceCell.html) and

[. A](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.OnceCell.html)

`sync::OnceCell``OnceCell` might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can
be assigned to at most once and provides direct access to the stored
contents. The core API looks *roughly*like this (and there’s much more inside, read on!):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T> OnceCell<T> {
    const fn new() -> OnceCell<T> { ... }
    fn set(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T> { ... }
    fn get(&self) -> Option<&T> { ... }
}
```
Note that, like with [ RefCell](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html) and

[, the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex``set` method requires
only a shared reference. Because of the single assignment restriction `get`
can return a `&T` instead of `Ref<T>` or `MutexGuard<T>`.The `sync` flavor is thread-safe (that is, implements the [ Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Sync.html) trait),
while the

`unsync` one is not.[§](https://docs.rs#recipes)Recipes

`OnceCell` might be useful for a variety of patterns.

[§](https://docs.rs#safe-initialization-of-global-data)Safe Initialization of Global Data

```
use std::{env, io};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Logger {
    // ...
}
static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Logger> = OnceCell::new();
impl Logger {
    pub fn global() -> &'static Logger {
        INSTANCE.get().expect("logger is not initialized")
    }
    fn from_cli(args: env::Args) -> Result<Logger, std::io::Error> {
       // ...
    }
}
fn main() {
    let logger = Logger::from_cli(env::args()).unwrap();
    INSTANCE.set(logger).unwrap();
    // use `Logger::global()` from now on
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazy-initialized-global-data)Lazy Initialized Global Data

This is essentially the `lazy_static!` macro, but without a macro.

```
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
fn global_data() -> &'static Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>> {
    static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = OnceCell::new();
    INSTANCE.get_or_init(|| {
        let mut m = HashMap::new();
        m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
        m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
        Mutex::new(m)
    })
}
```
There are also the [ sync::Lazy](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.Lazy.html) and

[convenience types to streamline this pattern:](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.Lazy.html)

`unsync::Lazy````
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA: Lazy<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = Lazy::new(|| {
    let mut m = HashMap::new();
    m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
    m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
    Mutex::new(m)
});
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", GLOBAL_DATA.lock().unwrap());
}
```
Note that the variable that holds `Lazy` is declared as `static`, *not*
`const`. This is important: using `const` instead compiles, but works wrong.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-purpose-lazy-evaluation)General purpose lazy evaluation

Unlike `lazy_static!`, `Lazy` works with local variables.

```
use once_cell::unsync::Lazy;
fn main() {
    let ctx = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let thunk = Lazy::new(|| {
        ctx.iter().sum::<i32>()
    });
    assert_eq!(*thunk, 6);
}
```
If you need a lazy field in a struct, you probably should use `OnceCell`
directly, because that will allow you to access `self` during
initialization.

```
use std::{fs, path::PathBuf};
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
struct Ctx {
    config_path: PathBuf,
    config: OnceCell<String>,
}
impl Ctx {
    pub fn get_config(&self) -> Result<&str, std::io::Error> {
        let cfg = self.config.get_or_try_init(|| {
            fs::read_to_string(&self.config_path)
        })?;
        Ok(cfg.as_str())
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazily-compiled-regex)Lazily Compiled Regex

This is a `regex!` macro which takes a string literal and returns an
*expression* that evaluates to a `&'static Regex`:

```
macro_rules! regex {
    ($re:literal $(,)?) => {{
        static RE: once_cell::sync::OnceCell<regex::Regex> = once_cell::sync::OnceCell::new();
        RE.get_or_init(|| regex::Regex::new($re).unwrap())
    }};
}
```
This macro can be useful to avoid the “compile regex on every loop iteration” problem.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-include_bytes)Runtime `include_bytes!`

The `include_bytes` macro is useful to include test resources, but it slows
down test compilation a lot. An alternative is to load the resources at
runtime:

```
use std::path::Path;
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct TestResource {
    path: &'static str,
    cell: OnceCell<Vec<u8>>,
}
impl TestResource {
    pub const fn new(path: &'static str) -> TestResource {
        TestResource { path, cell: OnceCell::new() }
    }
    pub fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        self.cell.get_or_init(|| {
            let dir = std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR").unwrap();
            let path = Path::new(dir.as_str()).join(self.path);
            std::fs::read(&path).unwrap_or_else(|_err| {
                panic!("failed to load test resource: {}", path.display())
            })
        }).as_slice()
    }
}
static TEST_IMAGE: TestResource = TestResource::new("test_data/lena.png");
#[test]
fn test_sobel_filter() {
    let rgb: &[u8] = TEST_IMAGE.bytes();
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lateinit)`lateinit`

`LateInit` type for delayed initialization. It is reminiscent of Kotlin’s
`lateinit` keyword and allows construction of cyclic data structures:

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct LateInit<T> { cell: OnceCell<T> }
impl<T> LateInit<T> {
    pub fn init(&self, value: T) {
        assert!(self.cell.set(value).is_ok())
    }
}
impl<T> Default for LateInit<T> {
    fn default() -> Self { LateInit { cell: OnceCell::default() } }
}
impl<T> std::ops::Deref for LateInit<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        self.cell.get().unwrap()
    }
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct A<'a> {
    b: LateInit<&'a B<'a>>,
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct B<'a> {
    a: LateInit<&'a A<'a>>
}
fn build_cycle() {
    let a = A::default();
    let b = B::default();
    a.b.init(&b);
    b.a.init(&a);
    let _a = &a.b.a.b.a;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-with-std)Comparison with std

| `!Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `Cell<T>` | `T` | requires `T: Copy`for`get` |
| `RefCell<T>` | `RefMut<T>`/`Ref<T>` | may panic at runtime |
| `unsync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once |

| `Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `AtomicT` | `T` | works only with certain `Copy`types |
| `Mutex<T>` | `MutexGuard<T>` | may deadlock at runtime, may block the thread |
| `sync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once, may block the thread |

Technically, calling `get_or_init` will also cause a panic or a deadlock if
it recursively calls itself. However, because the assignment can happen only
once, such cases should be more rare than equivalents with `RefCell` and
`Mutex`.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rustc-version)Minimum Supported `rustc` Version

If only the `std`, `alloc`, or `race` features are enabled, MSRV will be
updated conservatively, supporting at least latest 8 versions of the compiler.
When using other features, like `parking_lot`, MSRV might be updated more
frequently, up to the latest stable. In both cases, increasing MSRV is *not*
considered a semver-breaking change and requires only a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

The implementation is based on the
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/) and

[crates and](https://github.com/indiv0/lazycell/)

`lazy_cell`[. In some sense,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Once.html)

`std::sync::Once``once_cell` just streamlines and unifies
those APIs.To implement a sync flavor of `OnceCell`, this crates uses either a custom
re-implementation of `std::sync::Once` or `parking_lot::Mutex`. This is
controlled by the `parking_lot` feature (disabled by default). Performance
is the same for both cases, but the `parking_lot` based `OnceCell<T>` is
smaller by up to 16 bytes.

This crate uses `unsafe`.

[§](https://docs.rs#faq)F.A.Q.

**Should I use the sync or unsync flavor?**

Because Rust compiler checks thread safety for you, it’s impossible to
accidentally use `unsync` where `sync` is required. So, use `unsync` in
single-threaded code and `sync` in multi-threaded. It’s easy to switch
between the two if code becomes multi-threaded later.

At the moment, `unsync` has an additional benefit that reentrant
initialization causes a panic, which might be easier to debug than a
deadlock.

**Does this crate support async?**

No, but you can use
[ async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell) instead.

**Does this crate support  no_std?**

Yes, but with caveats. `OnceCell` is a synchronization primitive which
*semantically* relies on blocking. `OnceCell` guarantees that at most one
`f` will be called to compute the value. If two threads of execution call
`get_or_init` concurrently, one of them has to wait.

Waiting fundamentally requires OS support. Execution environment needs to
understand who waits on whom to prevent deadlocks due to priority inversion.
You *could* make code to compile by blindly using pure spinlocks, but the
runtime behavior would be subtly wrong.

Given these constraints, `once_cell` provides the following options:

- The `race`module provides similar, but distinct synchronization primitive which is compatible with`no_std`. With`race`, the`f`function can be called multiple times by different threads, but only one thread will win to install the value.
- `critical-section`feature (with a- `-`, not- `_`) uses- `critical_section`to implement blocking.

**Can I bring my own mutex?**

There is [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell) to
allow just that.

**Should I use  std::cell::OnceCell, once_cell, or lazy_static?**

If you can use `std` version (your MSRV is at least 1.70, and you don’t need
extra features `once_cell` provides), use `std`. Otherwise, use `once_cell`.
Don’t use `lazy_static`.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related crates

- Most of this crate’s functionality is available in `std`starting with Rust 1.70. See`std::cell::OnceCell`and`std::sync::OnceLock`.
- [double-checked-cell](https://github.com/niklasf/double-checked-cell)
- [lazy-init](https://crates.io/crates/lazy-init)
- [lazycell](https://crates.io/crates/lazycell)
- [mitochondria](https://crates.io/crates/mitochondria)
- [lazy_static](https://crates.io/crates/lazy_static)
- [async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell)
- [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell)(bring your own mutex)

        let mut m = HashMap::new();
        m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
        m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
        Mutex::new(m)
    })
}
```
There are also the [ sync::Lazy](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.Lazy.html) and

[convenience types to streamline this pattern:](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.Lazy.html)

`unsync::Lazy````
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA: Lazy<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = Lazy::new(|| {
    let mut m = HashMap::new();
    m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
    m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
    Mutex::new(m)
});
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", GLOBAL_DATA.lock().unwrap());
}
```
Note that the variable that holds `Lazy` is declared as `static`, *not*
`const`. This is important: using `const` instead compiles, but works wrong.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-purpose-lazy-evaluation)General purpose lazy evaluation

Unlike `lazy_static!`, `Lazy` works with local variables.

```
use once_cell::unsync::Lazy;
fn main() {
    let ctx = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let thunk = Lazy::new(|| {
        ctx.iter().sum::<i32>()
    });
    assert_eq!(*thunk, 6);
}
```
If you need a lazy field in a struct, you probably should use `OnceCell`
directly, because that will allow you to access `self` during
initialization.

```
use std::{fs, path::PathBuf};
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
struct Ctx {
    config_path: PathBuf,
    config: OnceCell<String>,
}
impl Ctx {
    pub fn get_config(&self) -> Result<&str, std::io::Error> {
        let cfg = self.config.get_or_try_init(|| {
            fs::read_to_string(&self.config_path)
        })?;
        Ok(cfg.as_str())
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazily-compiled-regex)Lazily Compiled Regex

This is a `regex!` macro which takes a string literal and returns an
*expression* that evaluates to a `&'static Regex`:

```
macro_rules! regex {
    ($re:literal $(,)?) => {{
        static RE: once_cell::sync::OnceCell<regex::Regex> = once_cell::sync::OnceCell::new();
        RE.get_or_init(|| regex::Regex::new($re).unwrap())
    }};
}
```
This macro can be useful to avoid the “compile regex on every loop iteration” problem.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-include_bytes)Runtime `include_bytes!`

The `include_bytes` macro is useful to include test resources, but it slows
down test compilation a lot. An alternative is to load the resources at
runtime:

```
use std::path::Path;
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct TestResource {
    path: &'static str,
    cell: OnceCell<Vec<u8>>,
}
impl TestResource {
    pub const fn new(path: &'static str) -> TestResource {
        TestResource { path, cell: OnceCell::new() }
    }
    pub fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        self.cell.get_or_init(|| {
            let dir = std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR").unwrap();
            let path = Path::new(dir.as_str()).join(self.path);
            std::fs::read(&path).unwrap_or_else(|_err| {
                panic!("failed to load test resource: {}", path.display())
            })
        }).as_slice()
    }
}
static TEST_IMAGE: TestResource = TestResource::new("test_data/lena.png");
#[test]
fn test_sobel_filter() {
    let rgb: &[u8] = TEST_IMAGE.bytes();
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lateinit)`lateinit`

`LateInit` type for delayed initialization. It is reminiscent of Kotlin’s
`lateinit` keyword and allows construction of cyclic data structures:

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct LateInit<T> { cell: OnceCell<T> }
impl<T> LateInit<T> {
    pub fn init(&self, value: T) {
        assert!(self.cell.set(value).is_ok())
    }
}
impl<T> Default for LateInit<T> {
    fn default() -> Self { LateInit { cell: OnceCell::default() } }
}
impl<T> std::ops::Deref for LateInit<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        self.cell.get().unwrap()
    }
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct A<'a> {
    b: LateInit<&'a B<'a>>,
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct B<'a> {
    a: LateInit<&'a A<'a>>
}
fn build_cycle() {
    let a = A::default();
    let b = B::default();
    a.b.init(&b);
    b.a.init(&a);
    let _a = &a.b.a.b.a;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-with-std)Comparison with std

| `!Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `Cell<T>` | `T` | requires `T: Copy`for`get` |
| `RefCell<T>` | `RefMut<T>`/`Ref<T>` | may panic at runtime |
| `unsync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once |

| `Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `AtomicT` | `T` | works only with certain `Copy`types |
| `Mutex<T>` | `MutexGuard<T>` | may deadlock at runtime, may block the thread |
| `sync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once, may block the thread |

Technically, calling `get_or_init` will also cause a panic or a deadlock if
it recursively calls itself. However, because the assignment can happen only
once, such cases should be more rare than equivalents with `RefCell` and
`Mutex`.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rustc-version)Minimum Supported `rustc` Version

If only the `std`, `alloc`, or `race` features are enabled, MSRV will be
updated conservatively, supporting at least latest 8 versions of the compiler.
When using other features, like `parking_lot`, MSRV might be updated more
frequently, up to the latest stable. In both cases, increasing MSRV is *not*
considered a semver-breaking change and requires only a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

The implementation is based on the
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/) and

[crates and](https://github.com/indiv0/lazycell/)

`lazy_cell`[. In some sense,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Once.html)

`std::sync::Once``once_cell` just streamlines and unifies
those APIs.To implement a sync flavor of `OnceCell`, this crates uses either a custom
re-implementation of `std::sync::Once` or `parking_lot::Mutex`. This is
controlled by the `parking_lot` feature (disabled by default). Performance
is the same for both cases, but the `parking_lot` based `OnceCell<T>` is
smaller by up to 16 bytes.

This crate uses `unsafe`.

[§](https://docs.rs#faq)F.A.Q.

**Should I use the sync or unsync flavor?**

Because Rust compiler checks thread safety for you, it’s impossible to
accidentally use `unsync` where `sync` is required. So, use `unsync` in
single-threaded code and `sync` in multi-threaded. It’s easy to switch
between the two if code becomes multi-threaded later.

At the moment, `unsync` has an additional benefit that reentrant
initialization causes a panic, which might be easier to debug than a
deadlock.

**Does this crate support async?**

No, but you can use
[ async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell) instead.

**Does this crate support  no_std?**

Yes, but with caveats. `OnceCell` is a synchronization primitive which
*semantically* relies on blocking. `OnceCell` guarantees that at most one
`f` will be called to compute the value. If two threads of execution call
`get_or_init` concurrently, one of them has to wait.

Waiting fundamentally requires OS support. Execution environment needs to
understand who waits on whom to prevent deadlocks due to priority inversion.
You *could* make code to compile by blindly using pure spinlocks, but the
runtime behavior would be subtly wrong.

Given these constraints, `once_cell` provides the following options:

- The `race`module provides similar, but distinct synchronization primitive which is compatible with`no_std`. With`race`, the`f`function can be called multiple times by different threads, but only one thread will win to install the value.
- `critical-section`feature (with a- `-`, not- `_`) uses- `critical_section`to implement blocking.

**Can I bring my own mutex?**

There is [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell) to
allow just that.

**Should I use  std::cell::OnceCell, once_cell, or lazy_static?**

If you can use `std` version (your MSRV is at least 1.70, and you don’t need
extra features `once_cell` provides), use `std`. Otherwise, use `once_cell`.
Don’t use `lazy_static`.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related crates

- Most of this crate’s functionality is available in `std`starting with Rust 1.70. See`std::cell::OnceCell`and`std::sync::OnceLock`.
- [double-checked-cell](https://github.com/niklasf/double-checked-cell)
- [lazy-init](https://crates.io/crates/lazy-init)
- [lazycell](https://crates.io/crates/lazycell)
- [mitochondria](https://crates.io/crates/mitochondria)
- [lazy_static](https://crates.io/crates/lazy_static)
- [async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell)
- [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell)(bring your own mutex)

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/1.21.4/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html

# once_cell/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Overview
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! `once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, [`unsync::OnceCell`] and
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [`sync::OnceCell`]. A `OnceCell` might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! be assigned to at most once and provides direct access to the stored
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! contents. The core API looks *roughly* like this (and there's much more
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! inside, read on!):
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ```rust,ignore
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! impl<T> OnceCell<T> {
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!     const fn new() -> OnceCell<T> { ... }
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!     fn set(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T> { ... }
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!     fn get(&self) -> Option<&T> { ... }
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! }
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! ```
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! Note that, like with [`RefCell`] and [`Mutex`], the `set` method requires
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! only a shared reference. Because of the single assignment restriction `get`
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! can return a `&T` instead of `Ref<T>` or `MutexGuard<T>`.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! The `sync` flavor is thread-safe (that is, implements the [`Sync`] trait),
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! while the `unsync` one is not.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! [`unsync::OnceCell`]: unsync/struct.OnceCell.html
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! [`sync::OnceCell`]: sync/struct.OnceCell.html
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! [`RefCell`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! [`Mutex`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [`Sync`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Sync.html
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! # Recipes
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! `OnceCell` might be useful for a variety of patterns.
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ## Safe Initialization of Global Data
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! ```rust
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! # #[cfg(any(feature = "std", feature = "critical-section"))] {
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! use std::{env, io};
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! #[derive(Debug)]
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! pub struct Logger {
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     // ...
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! }
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Logger> = OnceCell::new();
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! impl Logger {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     pub fn global() -> &'static Logger {
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!         INSTANCE.get().expect("logger is not initialized")
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     }
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     fn from_cli(args: env::Args) -> Result<Logger, std::io::Error> {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!        // ...
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! #      Ok(Logger {})
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!     }
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! }
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! fn main() {
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!     let logger = Logger::from_cli(env::args()).unwrap();
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!     INSTANCE.set(logger).unwrap();
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     // use `Logger::global()` from now on
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! }
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! # }
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! ```
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! ## Lazy Initialized Global Data
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! This is essentially the `lazy_static!` macro, but without a macro.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! ```rust
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! # #[cfg(any(feature = "std", feature = "critical-section"))] {
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! fn global_data() -> &'static Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>> {
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = OnceCell::new();
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!     INSTANCE.get_or_init(|| {
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!         let mut m = HashMap::new();
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!         m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!         m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!         Mutex::new(m)
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     })
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! }
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! # }
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! ```
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! There are also the [`sync::Lazy`] and [`unsync::Lazy`] convenience types to
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! streamline this pattern:
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! ```rust
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! # #[cfg(any(feature = "std", feature = "critical-section"))] {
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! static GLOBAL_DATA: Lazy<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = Lazy::new(|| {
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!     let mut m = HashMap::new();
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!     m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!     m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!     Mutex::new(m)
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! });
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! fn main() {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!     println!("{:?}", GLOBAL_DATA.lock().unwrap());
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! }
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! # }
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! ```
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! Note that the variable that holds `Lazy` is declared as `static`, *not*
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! `const`. This is important: using `const` instead compiles, but works wrong.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! [`sync::Lazy`]: sync/struct.Lazy.html
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! [`unsync::Lazy`]: unsync/struct.Lazy.html
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! ## General purpose lazy evaluation
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! Unlike `lazy_static!`, `Lazy` works with local variables.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! ```rust
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! use once_cell::unsync::Lazy;
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! fn main() {
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!     let ctx = vec![1, 2, 3];
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!     let thunk = Lazy::new(|| {
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!         ctx.iter().sum::<i32>()
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!     });
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!     assert_eq!(*thunk, 6);
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! }
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! ```
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! If you need a lazy field in a struct, you probably should use `OnceCell`
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! directly, because that will allow you to access `self` during
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! initialization.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! ```rust
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! use std::{fs, path::PathBuf};
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! struct Ctx {
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!     config_path: PathBuf,
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!     config: OnceCell<String>,
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! }
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! impl Ctx {
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!     pub fn get_config(&self) -> Result<&str, std::io::Error> {
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!         let cfg = self.config.get_or_try_init(|| {
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!             fs::read_to_string(&self.config_path)
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!         })?;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!         Ok(cfg.as_str())
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! ```
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! ## Lazily Compiled Regex
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! This is a `regex!` macro which takes a string literal and returns an
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! *expression* that evaluates to a `&'static Regex`:
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! ```
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! macro_rules! regex {
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!     ($re:literal $(,)?) => {{
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!         static RE: once_cell::sync::OnceCell<regex::Regex> = once_cell::sync::OnceCell::new();
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!         RE.get_or_init(|| regex::Regex::new($re).unwrap())
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!     }};
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! ```
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! This macro can be useful to avoid the "compile regex on every loop
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! iteration" problem.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! ## Runtime `include_bytes!`
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! The `include_bytes` macro is useful to include test resources, but it slows
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! down test compilation a lot. An alternative is to load the resources at
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! runtime:
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! ```
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! # #[cfg(any(feature = "std", feature = "critical-section"))] {
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! use std::path::Path;
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! pub struct TestResource {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!     path: &'static str,
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!     cell: OnceCell<Vec<u8>>,
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! impl TestResource {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!     pub const fn new(path: &'static str) -> TestResource {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!         TestResource { path, cell: OnceCell::new() }
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!     }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!     pub fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!         self.cell.get_or_init(|| {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!             let dir = std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR").unwrap();
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!             let path = Path::new(dir.as_str()).join(self.path);
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!             std::fs::read(&path).unwrap_or_else(|_err| {

[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!     }
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!

[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!

[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! fn test_sobel_filter() {

[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!     // ...
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! # drop(rgb);
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! # }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! ```
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! ## `lateinit`
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! `LateInit` type for delayed initialization. It is reminiscent of Kotlin's
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! `lateinit` keyword and allows construction of cyclic data structures:
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! ```
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! # #[cfg(any(feature = "std", feature = "critical-section"))] {
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! pub struct LateInit<T> { cell: OnceCell<T> }
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! impl<T> LateInit<T> {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//!     pub fn init(&self, value: T) {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//!         assert!(self.cell.set(value).is_ok())
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!     }
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! impl<T> Default for LateInit<T> {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!     fn default() -> Self { LateInit { cell: OnceCell::default() } }
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! }
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! impl<T> std::ops::Deref for LateInit<T> {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!     type Target = T;
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!     fn deref(&self) -> &T {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!         self.cell.get().unwrap()
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!     }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! #[derive(Default)]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! struct A<'a> {
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!     b: LateInit<&'a B<'a>>,
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! }
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! #[derive(Default)]
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! struct B<'a> {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!     a: LateInit<&'a A<'a>>
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! fn build_cycle() {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!     let a = A::default();
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!     let b = B::default();
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//!     a.b.init(&b);
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!     b.a.init(&a);
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!     let _a = &a.b.a.b.a;
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! }
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! # }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! ```
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! # Comparison with std
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! |`!Sync` types         | Access Mode            | Drawbacks                                     |
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! |----------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! |`Cell<T>`             | `T`                    | requires `T: Copy` for `get`                  |
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! |`RefCell<T>`          | `RefMut<T>` / `Ref<T>` | may panic at runtime                          |
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! |`unsync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T`                   | assignable only once                          |
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//!
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! |`Sync` types          | Access Mode            | Drawbacks                                     |
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! |----------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! |`AtomicT`             | `T`                    | works only with certain `Copy` types          |
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! |`Mutex<T>`            | `MutexGuard<T>`        | may deadlock at runtime, may block the thread |
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! |`sync::OnceCell<T>`   | `&T`                   | assignable only once, may block the thread    |
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! Technically, calling `get_or_init` will also cause a panic or a deadlock if
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! it recursively calls itself. However, because the assignment can happen only
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! once, such cases should be more rare than equivalents with `RefCell` and
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! `Mutex`.
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! # Minimum Supported `rustc` Version
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! If only the `std`, `alloc`, or `race` features are enabled, MSRV will be
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! updated conservatively, supporting at least latest 8 versions of the compiler.
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! When using other features, like `parking_lot`, MSRV might be updated more
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! frequently, up to the latest stable. In both cases, increasing MSRV is *not*
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! considered a semver-breaking change and requires only a minor version bump.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! # Implementation details
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! The implementation is based on the
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! [`lazy_static`](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/) and
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! [`lazy_cell`](https://github.com/indiv0/lazycell/) crates and
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! [`std::sync::Once`]. In some sense, `once_cell` just streamlines and unifies
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! those APIs.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! To implement a sync flavor of `OnceCell`, this crates uses either a custom
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! re-implementation of `std::sync::Once` or `parking_lot::Mutex`. This is
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! controlled by the `parking_lot` feature (disabled by default). Performance
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! is the same for both cases, but the `parking_lot` based `OnceCell<T>` is
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! smaller by up to 16 bytes.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! This crate uses `unsafe`.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! [`std::sync::Once`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Once.html
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! # F.A.Q.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! **Should I use the sync or unsync flavor?**
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! Because Rust compiler checks thread safety for you, it's impossible to
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//! accidentally use `unsync` where `sync` is required. So, use `unsync` in
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! single-threaded code and `sync` in multi-threaded. It's easy to switch
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! between the two if code becomes multi-threaded later.
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! At the moment, `unsync` has an additional benefit that reentrant
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! initialization causes a panic, which might be easier to debug than a
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//! deadlock.
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! **Does this crate support async?**
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! No, but you can use
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! [`async_once_cell`](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell) instead.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! **Does this crate support `no_std`?**
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! Yes, but with caveats. `OnceCell` is a synchronization primitive which
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! _semantically_ relies on blocking. `OnceCell` guarantees that at most one
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//! `f` will be called to compute the value. If two threads of execution call
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! `get_or_init` concurrently, one of them has to wait.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! Waiting fundamentally requires OS support. Execution environment needs to
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//! understand who waits on whom to prevent deadlocks due to priority inversion.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! You _could_ make code to compile by blindly using pure spinlocks, but the
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! runtime behavior would be subtly wrong.
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! Given these constraints, `once_cell` provides the following options:
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//!
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! - The `race` module provides similar, but distinct synchronization primitive
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//!   which is compatible with `no_std`. With `race`, the `f` function can be
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!   called multiple times by different threads, but only one thread will win
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!   to install the value.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! - `critical-section` feature (with a `-`, not `_`) uses `critical_section`
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//!   to implement blocking.
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//! **Can I bring my own mutex?**
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//! There is [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell) to
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//! allow just that.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//!
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//! **Should I use `std::cell::OnceCell`, `once_cell`, or `lazy_static`?**
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//!
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//! If you can use `std` version (your MSRV is at least 1.70, and you don't need
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//! extra features `once_cell` provides), use `std`. Otherwise, use `once_cell`.
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//! Don't use `lazy_static`.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//! # Related crates
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//! * Most of this crate's functionality is available in `std` starting with
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!   Rust 1.70. See `std::cell::OnceCell` and `std::sync::OnceLock`.
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//! * [double-checked-cell](https://github.com/niklasf/double-checked-cell)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//! * [lazy-init](https://crates.io/crates/lazy-init)
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//! * [lazycell](https://crates.io/crates/lazycell)
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//! * [mitochondria](https://crates.io/crates/mitochondria)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//! * [lazy_static](https://crates.io/crates/lazy_static)
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//! * [async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell)
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//! * [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell) (bring
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//!   your own mutex)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)
