[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// A cell which can be written to only once. It is not thread safe.
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// Unlike [`std::cell::RefCell`], a `OnceCell` provides simple `&`
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// references to the contents.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// [`std::cell::RefCell`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    ///
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// # Example
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// ```
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// let cell = OnceCell::new();
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// assert!(cell.get().is_none());
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// let value: &String = cell.get_or_init(|| {
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    ///     "Hello, World!".to_string()
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// });
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// assert_eq!(value, "Hello, World!");
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// assert!(cell.get().is_some());
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// ```
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    pub struct [OnceCell](https://docs.rs/once_cell/unsync/struct.OnceCell.html)<T> {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        // Invariant: written to at most once.
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        inner: [UnsafeCell](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cell/struct.UnsafeCell.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>>,
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    }

[493](https://docs.rs#493)        pub fn get(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&T> {
[494](https://docs.rs#494)            // Safe due to `inner`'s invariant of being written to at most once.
[495](https://docs.rs#495)            // Had multiple writes to `inner` been allowed, a reference to the

[497](https://docs.rs#497)            // different value later.

[501](https://docs.rs#501)        /// Gets a mutable reference to the underlying value.
[502](https://docs.rs#502)        ///
[503](https://docs.rs#503)        /// Returns `None` if the cell is empty.
[504](https://docs.rs#504)        ///
[505](https://docs.rs#505)        /// This method is allowed to violate the invariant of writing to a `OnceCell`
[506](https://docs.rs#506)        /// at most once because it requires `&mut` access to `self`. As with all
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        /// interior mutability, `&mut` access permits arbitrary modification:
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        ///
[509](https://docs.rs#509)        /// ```
[510](https://docs.rs#510)        /// use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        ///
[512](https://docs.rs#512)        /// let mut cell: OnceCell<u32> = OnceCell::new();
[513](https://docs.rs#513)        /// cell.set(92).unwrap();
[514](https://docs.rs#514)        /// *cell.get_mut().unwrap() = 93;
[515](https://docs.rs#515)        /// assert_eq!(cell.get(), Some(&93));
[516](https://docs.rs#516)        /// ```
[517](https://docs.rs#517)        #[inline]
[518](https://docs.rs#518)        pub fn get_mut(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&mut T> {
[519](https://docs.rs#519)            // Safe because we have unique access
[520](https://docs.rs#520)            unsafe { &mut *[self](https://docs.rs#518).inner.[get](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cell/struct.UnsafeCell.html#method.get)() }.[as_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#method.as_mut)()
[521](https://docs.rs#521)        }

[523](https://docs.rs#523)        /// Sets the contents of this cell to `value`.
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        ///
[525](https://docs.rs#525)        /// Returns `Ok(())` if the cell was empty and `Err(value)` if it was
[526](https://docs.rs#526)        /// full.
[527](https://docs.rs#527)        ///
[528](https://docs.rs#528)        /// # Example
[529](https://docs.rs#529)        /// ```
[530](https://docs.rs#530)        /// use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[531](https://docs.rs#531)        ///
[532](https://docs.rs#532)        /// let cell = OnceCell::new();
[533](https://docs.rs#533)        /// assert!(cell.get().is_none());
[534](https://docs.rs#534)        ///
[535](https://docs.rs#535)        /// assert_eq!(cell.set(92), Ok(()));
[536](https://docs.rs#536)        /// assert_eq!(cell.set(62), Err(62));
[537](https://docs.rs#537)        ///
[538](https://docs.rs#538)        /// assert!(cell.get().is_some());
[539](https://docs.rs#539)        /// ```
[540](https://docs.rs#540)        pub fn set(&self, value: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<(), T> {
[541](https://docs.rs#541)            match [self](https://docs.rs#540).[try_insert](https://docs.rs#561-573)([value](https://docs.rs#540)) {
[542](https://docs.rs#542)                [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(_) => [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(()),
[543](https://docs.rs#543)                [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)((_, value)) => [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)([value](https://docs.rs#543)),
[544](https://docs.rs#544)            }
[545](https://docs.rs#545)        }

[547](https://docs.rs#547)        /// Like [`set`](Self::set), but also returns a reference to the final cell value.
[548](https://docs.rs#548)        ///
[549](https://docs.rs#549)        /// # Example
[550](https://docs.rs#550)        /// ```
[551](https://docs.rs#551)        /// use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[552](https://docs.rs#552)        ///
[553](https://docs.rs#553)        /// let cell = OnceCell::new();
[554](https://docs.rs#554)        /// assert!(cell.get().is_none());
[555](https://docs.rs#555)        ///
[556](https://docs.rs#556)        /// assert_eq!(cell.try_insert(92), Ok(&92));
[557](https://docs.rs#557)        /// assert_eq!(cell.try_insert(62), Err((&92, 62)));
[558](https://docs.rs#558)        ///
[559](https://docs.rs#559)        /// assert!(cell.get().is_some());
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        /// ```
[561](https://docs.rs#561)        pub fn try_insert(&self, value: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<&T, (&T, T)> {
[562](https://docs.rs#562)            if let [Some](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)(old) = [self](https://docs.rs#561).[get](https://docs.rs#493-499)() {
[563](https://docs.rs#563)                return [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)(([old](https://docs.rs#562), [value](https://docs.rs#561)));
[564](https://docs.rs#564)            }
[565](https://docs.rs#565)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)            let slot = unsafe { &mut *[self](https://docs.rs#561).inner.[get](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cell/struct.UnsafeCell.html#method.get)() };
[567](https://docs.rs#567)            // This is the only place where we set the slot, no races
[568](https://docs.rs#568)            // due to reentrancy/concurrency are possible, and we've
[569](https://docs.rs#569)            // checked that slot is currently `None`, so this write
[570](https://docs.rs#570)            // maintains the `inner`'s invariant.
[571](https://docs.rs#571)            *[slot](https://docs.rs#566) = [Some](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)([value](https://docs.rs#561));
[572](https://docs.rs#572)            [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(unsafe { [slot](https://docs.rs#566).[as_ref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#method.as_ref)().[unwrap_unchecked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#method.unwrap_unchecked)() })
[573](https://docs.rs#573)        }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)
[575](https://docs.rs#575)        /// Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f`
[576](https://docs.rs#576)        /// if the cell was empty.
[577](https://docs.rs#577)        ///
[578](https://docs.rs#578)        /// # Panics
[579](https://docs.rs#579)        ///
[580](https://docs.rs#580)        /// If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and the cell
[581](https://docs.rs#581)        /// remains uninitialized.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)        ///
[583](https://docs.rs#583)        /// It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`. Doing
[584](https://docs.rs#584)        /// so results in a panic.
[585](https://docs.rs#585)        ///
[586](https://docs.rs#586)        /// # Example
[587](https://docs.rs#587)        /// ```
[588](https://docs.rs#588)        /// use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[589](https://docs.rs#589)        ///
[590](https://docs.rs#590)        /// let cell = OnceCell::new();
[591](https://docs.rs#591)        /// let value = cell.get_or_init(|| 92);
[592](https://docs.rs#592)        /// assert_eq!(value, &92);
[593](https://docs.rs#593)        /// let value = cell.get_or_init(|| unreachable!());
[594](https://docs.rs#594)        /// assert_eq!(value, &92);
[595](https://docs.rs#595)        /// ```
[596](https://docs.rs#596)        pub fn get_or_init<F>(&self, f: F) -> &T
[597](https://docs.rs#597)        where
[598](https://docs.rs#598)            F: [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)() -> T,
[599](https://docs.rs#599)        {
[600](https://docs.rs#600)            enum Void {}
[601](https://docs.rs#601)            match [self](https://docs.rs#596).[get_or_try_init](https://docs.rs#632-646)(|| [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)::<T, [Void](https://docs.rs#600)>([f](https://docs.rs#596)())) {
[602](https://docs.rs#602)                [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(val) => [val](https://docs.rs#602),
[603](https://docs.rs#603)                [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)(void) => match [void](https://docs.rs#603) {},
[604](https://docs.rs#604)            }
[605](https://docs.rs#605)        }
[606](https://docs.rs#606)
[607](https://docs.rs#607)        /// Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f` if
[608](https://docs.rs#608)        /// the cell was empty. If the cell was empty and `f` failed, an
[609](https://docs.rs#609)        /// error is returned.
[610](https://docs.rs#610)        ///
[611](https://docs.rs#611)        /// # Panics
[612](https://docs.rs#612)        ///
[613](https://docs.rs#613)        /// If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and the cell
[614](https://docs.rs#614)        /// remains uninitialized.
[615](https://docs.rs#615)        ///
[616](https://docs.rs#616)        /// It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`. Doing
[617](https://docs.rs#617)        /// so results in a panic.
[618](https://docs.rs#618)        ///
[619](https://docs.rs#619)        /// # Example
[620](https://docs.rs#620)        /// ```
[621](https://docs.rs#621)        /// use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        ///
[623](https://docs.rs#623)        /// let cell = OnceCell::new();
[624](https://docs.rs#624)        /// assert_eq!(cell.get_or_try_init(|| Err(())), Err(()));
[625](https://docs.rs#625)        /// assert!(cell.get().is_none());
[626](https://docs.rs#626)        /// let value = cell.get_or_try_init(|| -> Result<i32, ()> {
[627](https://docs.rs#627)        ///     Ok(92)
[628](https://docs.rs#628)        /// });
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        /// assert_eq!(value, Ok(&92));
[630](https://docs.rs#630)        /// assert_eq!(cell.get(), Some(&92))
[631](https://docs.rs#631)        /// ```
[632](https://docs.rs#632)        pub fn get_or_try_init<F, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<&T, E>
[633](https://docs.rs#633)        where
[634](https://docs.rs#634)            F: [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)() -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>,
[635](https://docs.rs#635)        {
[636](https://docs.rs#636)            if let [Some](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)(val) = [self](https://docs.rs#632).[get](https://docs.rs#493-499)() {
[637](https://docs.rs#637)                return [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)([val](https://docs.rs#636));
[638](https://docs.rs#638)            }
[639](https://docs.rs#639)            let val = f()?;
[640](https://docs.rs#640)            // Note that *some* forms of reentrant initialization might lead to
[641](https://docs.rs#641)            // UB (see `reentrant_init` test). I believe that just removing this
[642](https://docs.rs#642)            // `assert`, while keeping `set/get` would be sound, but it seems
[643](https://docs.rs#643)            // better to panic, rather than to silently use an old value.
[644](https://docs.rs#644)            [assert!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.assert.html)(self.set(val).is_ok(), "reentrant init");
[645](https://docs.rs#645)            [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(unsafe { [self](https://docs.rs#632).[get](https://docs.rs#493-499)().[unwrap_unchecked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#method.unwrap_unchecked)() })
[646](https://docs.rs#646)        }
[647](https://docs.rs#647)
[648](https://docs.rs#648)        /// Takes the value out of this `OnceCell`, moving it back to an uninitialized state.

[668](https://docs.rs#668)        /// interior mutability, `&mut` access permits arbitrary modification:
[669](https://docs.rs#669)        ///
[670](https://docs.rs#670)        /// ```
[671](https://docs.rs#671)        /// use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
[672](https://docs.rs#672)        ///
[673](https://docs.rs#673)        /// let mut cell: OnceCell<u32> = OnceCell::new();
[674](https://docs.rs#674)        /// cell.set(92).unwrap();
[675](https://docs.rs#675)        /// cell = OnceCell::new();
[676](https://docs.rs#676)        /// ```

[882](https://docs.rs#882)
[883](https://docs.rs#883)    /// A thread-safe cell which can be written to only once.
[884](https://docs.rs#884)    ///
[885](https://docs.rs#885)    /// `OnceCell` provides `&` references to the contents without RAII guards.
[886](https://docs.rs#886)    ///
[887](https://docs.rs#887)    /// Reading a non-`None` value out of `OnceCell` establishes a
[888](https://docs.rs#888)    /// happens-before relationship with a corresponding write. For example, if
[889](https://docs.rs#889)    /// thread A initializes the cell with `get_or_init(f)`, and thread B
[890](https://docs.rs#890)    /// subsequently reads the result of this call, B also observes all the side
[891](https://docs.rs#891)    /// effects of `f`.
[892](https://docs.rs#892)    ///
[893](https://docs.rs#893)    /// # Example
[894](https://docs.rs#894)    /// ```
[895](https://docs.rs#895)    /// use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
[896](https://docs.rs#896)    ///
[897](https://docs.rs#897)    /// static CELL: OnceCell<String> = OnceCell::new();
[898](https://docs.rs#898)    /// assert!(CELL.get().is_none());
[899](https://docs.rs#899)    ///
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    /// std::thread::spawn(|| {
[901](https://docs.rs#901)    ///     let value: &String = CELL.get_or_init(|| {
[902](https://docs.rs#902)    ///         "Hello, World!".to_string()
[903](https://docs.rs#903)    ///     });
[904](https://docs.rs#904)    ///     assert_eq!(value, "Hello, World!");
[905](https://docs.rs#905)    /// }).join().unwrap();
[906](https://docs.rs#906)    ///
[907](https://docs.rs#907)    /// let value: Option<&String> = CELL.get();
[908](https://docs.rs#908)    /// assert!(value.is_some());
[909](https://docs.rs#909)    /// assert_eq!(value.unwrap().as_str(), "Hello, World!");
[910](https://docs.rs#910)    /// ```
[911](https://docs.rs#911)    pub struct [OnceCell](https://docs.rs/once_cell/sync/struct.OnceCell.html)<T>([Imp](https://docs.rs/imp_pl.rs.html#7-10)<T>);
[912](https://docs.rs#912)
[913](https://docs.rs#913)    impl<T> [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) for [OnceCell](https://docs.rs#911)<T> {

[982](https://docs.rs#982)        /// Gets the reference to the underlying value, blocking the current
[983](https://docs.rs#983)        /// thread until it is set.
[984](https://docs.rs#984)        ///
[985](https://docs.rs#985)        /// ```
[986](https://docs.rs#986)        /// use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
[987](https://docs.rs#987)        ///
[988](https://docs.rs#988)        /// let mut cell = std::sync::Arc::new(OnceCell::new());
[989](https://docs.rs#989)        /// let t = std::thread::spawn({
[990](https://docs.rs#990)        ///     let cell = std::sync::Arc::clone(&cell);
[991](https://docs.rs#991)        ///     move || cell.set(92).unwrap()
[992](https://docs.rs#992)        /// });

[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)        /// t.join().unwrap();

[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)                [self](https://docs.rs#1003).0.[wait](https://docs.rs/imp_pl.rs.html#80-94)()
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)            }
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)            [debug_assert!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.debug_assert.html)(self.0.is_initialized());
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)            // Safe b/c of the wait call above and the fact that we didn't
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)            // relinquish our borrow.
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)            unsafe { [self](https://docs.rs#1003).[get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#1041-1043)() }
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)        }

[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)        /// Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f` if the cell
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)        /// was empty.
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)        ///
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)        /// Many threads may call `get_or_init` concurrently with different
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)        /// initializing functions, but it is guaranteed that only one function
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)        /// will be executed.
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)        ///
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)        /// # Panics
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)        ///
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)        /// If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and the cell
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)        /// remains uninitialized.
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)        ///
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)        /// It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`. The
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)        /// exact outcome is unspecified. Current implementation deadlocks, but
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)        /// this may be changed to a panic in the future.
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)        ///
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)        /// # Example
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)        /// ```
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)        /// use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)        ///
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)        /// let cell = OnceCell::new();
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)        /// let value = cell.get_or_init(|| 92);
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)        /// assert_eq!(value, &92);
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)        /// let value = cell.get_or_init(|| unreachable!());
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)        /// assert_eq!(value, &92);
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)        /// ```
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)        pub fn get_or_init<F>(&self, f: F) -> &T
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)        where
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)            F: [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)() -> T,
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)        {
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)            enum Void {}
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)            match [self](https://docs.rs#1125).[get_or_try_init](https://docs.rs#1162-1176)(|| [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)::<T, [Void](https://docs.rs#1129)>([f](https://docs.rs#1125)())) {
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)                [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(val) => [val](https://docs.rs#1131),
[1132](https://docs.rs#1132)                [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)(void) => match [void](https://docs.rs#1132) {},
[1133](https://docs.rs#1133)            }
[1134](https://docs.rs#1134)        }
[1135](https://docs.rs#1135)
[1136](https://docs.rs#1136)        /// Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f` if
[1137](https://docs.rs#1137)        /// the cell was empty. If the cell was empty and `f` failed, an
[1138](https://docs.rs#1138)        /// error is returned.
[1139](https://docs.rs#1139)        ///
[1140](https://docs.rs#1140)        /// # Panics
[1141](https://docs.rs#1141)        ///
[1142](https://docs.rs#1142)        /// If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and
[1143](https://docs.rs#1143)        /// the cell remains uninitialized.
[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)        ///
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)        /// It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`.
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)        /// The exact outcome is unspecified. Current implementation
[1147](https://docs.rs#1147)        /// deadlocks, but this may be changed to a panic in the future.
[1148](https://docs.rs#1148)        ///
[1149](https://docs.rs#1149)        /// # Example

[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)        /// let cell = OnceCell::new();
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)        /// assert_eq!(cell.get_or_try_init(|| Err(())), Err(()));
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)        /// assert!(cell.get().is_none());
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)        /// let value = cell.get_or_try_init(|| -> Result<i32, ()> {
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)        ///     Ok(92)
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)        /// });
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)        /// assert_eq!(value, Ok(&92));
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)        /// assert_eq!(cell.get(), Some(&92))
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)        /// ```
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)        pub fn get_or_try_init<F, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<&T, E>
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)        where
[1164](https://docs.rs#1164)            F: [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)() -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>,
[1165](https://docs.rs#1165)        {
[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)            // Fast path check
[1167](https://docs.rs#1167)            if let [Some](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)(value) = [self](https://docs.rs#1162).[get](https://docs.rs#973-980)() {

[1169](https://docs.rs#1169)            }
[1170](https://docs.rs#1170)
[1171](https://docs.rs#1171)            self.0.initialize(f)?;
[1172](https://docs.rs#1172)
[1173](https://docs.rs#1173)            // Safe b/c value is initialized.
[1174](https://docs.rs#1174)            [debug_assert!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.debug_assert.html)(self.0.is_initialized());
[1175](https://docs.rs#1175)            [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(unsafe { [self](https://docs.rs#1162).[get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#1041-1043)() })
[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)        }

[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)    /// A value which is initialized on the first access.
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)    ///
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)    /// This type is thread-safe and can be used in statics.
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)    ///
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)    /// # Example
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)    ///
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)    /// ```
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)    /// use std::collections::HashMap;
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)    ///
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)    /// use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)    ///
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)    /// static HASHMAP: Lazy<HashMap<i32, String>> = Lazy::new(|| {
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)    ///     println!("initializing");
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)    ///     let mut m = HashMap::new();
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)    ///     m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)    ///     m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)    ///     m
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)    /// });
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)    ///
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)    /// fn main() {
[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)    ///     println!("ready");
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)    ///     std::thread::spawn(|| {
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)    ///         println!("{:?}", HASHMAP.get(&13));
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)    ///     }).join().unwrap();
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)    ///     println!("{:?}", HASHMAP.get(&74));
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)    ///
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)    ///     // Prints:
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)    ///     //   ready
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)    ///     //   initializing
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)    ///     //   Some("Spica")
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)    ///     //   Some("Hoyten")
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)    /// }

# OnceCell in once_cell::unsync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/1.21.4/once_cell/unsync/struct.OnceCell.html

`pub struct OnceCell<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A cell which can be written to only once. It is not thread safe.

Unlike [ std::cell::RefCell](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html), a

`OnceCell` provides simple `&`
references to the contents.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
let cell = OnceCell::new();
assert!(cell.get().is_none());
let value: &String = cell.get_or_init(|| {
    "Hello, World!".to_string()
});
assert_eq!(value, "Hello, World!");
assert!(cell.get().is_some());
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Gets a reference to the underlying value.

Returns `None` if the cell is empty.

Gets a mutable reference to the underlying value.

Returns `None` if the cell is empty.

This method is allowed to violate the invariant of writing to a `OnceCell`
at most once because it requires `&mut` access to `self`. As with all
interior mutability, `&mut` access permits arbitrary modification:

```
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
let mut cell: OnceCell<u32> = OnceCell::new();
cell.set(92).unwrap();
*cell.get_mut().unwrap() = 93;
assert_eq!(cell.get(), Some(&93));
```
Sets the contents of this cell to `value`.

Returns `Ok(())` if the cell was empty and `Err(value)` if it was
full.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
let cell = OnceCell::new();
assert!(cell.get().is_none());
assert_eq!(cell.set(92), Ok(()));
assert_eq!(cell.set(62), Err(62));
assert!(cell.get().is_some());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#596-605)#### pub fn [get_or_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_init)<F>(&self, f: F) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#596-605)

#### pub fn [get_or_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_init)<F>(&self, f: F) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f`
if the cell was empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and the cell
remains uninitialized.

It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`. Doing
so results in a panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
let cell = OnceCell::new();
let value = cell.get_or_init(|| 92);
assert_eq!(value, &92);
let value = cell.get_or_init(|| unreachable!());
assert_eq!(value, &92);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#632-646)#### pub fn [get_or_try_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_try_init)<F, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#632-646)

#### pub fn [get_or_try_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_try_init)<F, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), E>

Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f` if
the cell was empty. If the cell was empty and `f` failed, an
error is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and the cell
remains uninitialized.

It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`. Doing
so results in a panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
let cell = OnceCell::new();
assert_eq!(cell.get_or_try_init(|| Err(())), Err(()));
assert!(cell.get().is_none());
let value = cell.get_or_try_init(|| -> Result<i32, ()> {
    Ok(92)
});
assert_eq!(value, Ok(&92));
assert_eq!(cell.get(), Some(&92))
```
Takes the value out of this `OnceCell`, moving it back to an uninitialized state.

Has no effect and returns `None` if the `OnceCell` hasn’t been initialized.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
let mut cell: OnceCell<String> = OnceCell::new();
assert_eq!(cell.take(), None);
let mut cell = OnceCell::new();
cell.set("hello".to_string()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(cell.take(), Some("hello".to_string()));
assert_eq!(cell.get(), None);
```
This method is allowed to violate the invariant of writing to a `OnceCell`
at most once because it requires `&mut` access to `self`. As with all
interior mutability, `&mut` access permits arbitrary modification:

```
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
let mut cell: OnceCell<u32> = OnceCell::new();
cell.set(92).unwrap();
cell = OnceCell::new();
```

Consumes the `OnceCell`, returning the wrapped value.

Returns `None` if the cell was empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

assert_eq!(cell.into_inner(), None);
let cell = OnceCell::new();
cell.set("hello".to_string()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(cell.into_inner(), Some("hello".to_string()));
```

# OnceCell in once_cell::sync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/1.21.4/once_cell/sync/struct.OnceCell.html

`pub struct OnceCell<T>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A thread-safe cell which can be written to only once.

`OnceCell` provides `&` references to the contents without RAII guards.

Reading a non-`None` value out of `OnceCell` establishes a
happens-before relationship with a corresponding write. For example, if
thread A initializes the cell with `get_or_init(f)`, and thread B
subsequently reads the result of this call, B also observes all the side
effects of `f`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
static CELL: OnceCell<String> = OnceCell::new();
assert!(CELL.get().is_none());
std::thread::spawn(|| {
    let value: &String = CELL.get_or_init(|| {
        "Hello, World!".to_string()
    });
    assert_eq!(value, "Hello, World!");
}).join().unwrap();
let value: Option<&String> = CELL.get();
assert!(value.is_some());
assert_eq!(value.unwrap().as_str(), "Hello, World!");
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Gets the reference to the underlying value.

Returns `None` if the cell is empty, or being initialized. This
method never blocks.

Gets the reference to the underlying value, blocking the current thread until it is set.

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
let mut cell = std::sync::Arc::new(OnceCell::new());
let t = std::thread::spawn({
    let cell = std::sync::Arc::clone(&cell);
    move || cell.set(92).unwrap()
});
// Returns immediately, but might return None.
let _value_or_none = cell.get();
// Will return 92, but might block until the other thread does `.set`.
let value: &u32 = cell.wait();
assert_eq!(*value, 92);
t.join().unwrap();
```
Gets the mutable reference to the underlying value.

Returns `None` if the cell is empty.

This method is allowed to violate the invariant of writing to a `OnceCell`
at most once because it requires `&mut` access to `self`. As with all
interior mutability, `&mut` access permits arbitrary modification:

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
let mut cell: OnceCell<u32> = OnceCell::new();
cell.set(92).unwrap();
cell = OnceCell::new();
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#1041-1043)#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_unchecked)(&self) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#1041-1043)

#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_unchecked)(&self) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

Get the reference to the underlying value, without checking if the cell is initialized.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Caller must ensure that the cell is in initialized state, and that the contents are acquired by (synchronized to) this thread.

Sets the contents of this cell to `value`.

Returns `Ok(())` if the cell was empty and `Err(value)` if it was
full.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
static CELL: OnceCell<i32> = OnceCell::new();
fn main() {
    assert!(CELL.get().is_none());
    std::thread::spawn(|| {
        assert_eq!(CELL.set(92), Ok(()));
    }).join().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(CELL.set(62), Err(62));
    assert_eq!(CELL.get(), Some(&92));
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#1125-1134)#### pub fn [get_or_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_init)<F>(&self, f: F) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#1125-1134)

#### pub fn [get_or_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_init)<F>(&self, f: F) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f` if the cell
was empty.

Many threads may call `get_or_init` concurrently with different
initializing functions, but it is guaranteed that only one function
will be executed.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and the cell
remains uninitialized.

It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`. The
exact outcome is unspecified. Current implementation deadlocks, but
this may be changed to a panic in the future.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
let cell = OnceCell::new();
let value = cell.get_or_init(|| 92);
assert_eq!(value, &92);
let value = cell.get_or_init(|| unreachable!());
assert_eq!(value, &92);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#1162-1176)#### pub fn [get_or_try_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_try_init)<F, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/once_cell/lib.rs.html#1162-1176)

#### pub fn [get_or_try_init](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_try_init)<F, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), E>

Gets the contents of the cell, initializing it with `f` if
the cell was empty. If the cell was empty and `f` failed, an
error is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

If `f` panics, the panic is propagated to the caller, and
the cell remains uninitialized.

It is an error to reentrantly initialize the cell from `f`.
The exact outcome is unspecified. Current implementation
deadlocks, but this may be changed to a panic in the future.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
let cell = OnceCell::new();
assert_eq!(cell.get_or_try_init(|| Err(())), Err(()));
assert!(cell.get().is_none());
let value = cell.get_or_try_init(|| -> Result<i32, ()> {
    Ok(92)
});
assert_eq!(value, Ok(&92));
assert_eq!(cell.get(), Some(&92))
```
Takes the value out of this `OnceCell`, moving it back to an uninitialized state.

Has no effect and returns `None` if the `OnceCell` hasn’t been initialized.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
let mut cell: OnceCell<String> = OnceCell::new();
assert_eq!(cell.take(), None);
let mut cell = OnceCell::new();
cell.set("hello".to_string()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(cell.take(), Some("hello".to_string()));
assert_eq!(cell.get(), None);
```

```

cell.set(92).unwrap();

# Lazy in once_cell::sync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/1.21.4/once_cell/sync/struct.Lazy.html

`pub struct Lazy<T, F = `[fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.fn.html)() -> T> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A value which is initialized on the first access.

This type is thread-safe and can be used in statics.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::collections::HashMap;
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
static HASHMAP: Lazy<HashMap<i32, String>> = Lazy::new(|| {
    println!("initializing");
    let mut m = HashMap::new();
    m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
    m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
    m
});
fn main() {
    println!("ready");
    std::thread::spawn(|| {
        println!("{:?}", HASHMAP.get(&13));
    }).join().unwrap();
    println!("{:?}", HASHMAP.get(&74));
    // Prints:
    //   ready
    //   initializing
    //   Some("Spica")
    //   Some("Hoyten")
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Forces the evaluation of this lazy value and
returns a reference to the result. This is equivalent
to the `Deref` impl, but is explicit.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
let lazy = Lazy::new(|| 92);
assert_eq!(Lazy::force(&lazy), &92);
assert_eq!(&*lazy, &92);
```
Forces the evaluation of this lazy value and
returns a mutable reference to the result. This is equivalent
to the `Deref` impl, but is explicit.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
let mut lazy = Lazy::new(|| 92);
assert_eq!(Lazy::force_mut(&mut lazy), &mut 92);
```
Gets the reference to the result of this lazy value if
it was initialized, otherwise returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
let lazy = Lazy::new(|| 92);
assert_eq!(Lazy::get(&lazy), None);
assert_eq!(&*lazy, &92);
assert_eq!(Lazy::get(&lazy), Some(&92));
```
Gets the reference to the result of this lazy value if
it was initialized, otherwise returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
let mut lazy = Lazy::new(|| 92);
assert_eq!(Lazy::get_mut(&mut lazy), None);
assert_eq!(&*lazy, &92);
assert_eq!(Lazy::get_mut(&mut lazy), Some(&mut 92));
```

# once_cell::race - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/1.21.4/once_cell/race/index.html

## Expand description

Thread-safe, non-blocking, “first one wins” flavor of `OnceCell`.

If two threads race to initialize a type from the `race` module, they
don’t block, execute initialization function together, but only one of
them stores the result.

This module does not require `std` feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#atomic-orderings)Atomic orderings

All types in this module use `Acquire` and `Release`
[atomic orderings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/enum.Ordering.html) for all their operations. While this is not
strictly necessary for types other than `OnceBox`, it is useful for users as
it allows them to be certain that after `get` or `get_or_init` returns on
one thread, any side-effects caused by the setter thread prior to them
calling `set` or `get_or_init` will be made visible to that thread; without
it, it’s possible for it to appear as if they haven’t happened yet from the
getter thread’s perspective. This is an acceptable tradeoff to make since
`Acquire` and `Release` have very little performance overhead on most
architectures versus `Relaxed`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Once](https://docs.rs/struct.OnceBool.html)- Bool
- A thread-safe cell which can be written to only once.
- [OnceBox](https://docs.rs/struct.OnceBox.html)
- A thread-safe cell which can be written to only once.
- [Once](https://docs.rs/struct.OnceNonZeroUsize.html)- NonZero - Usize
- A thread-safe cell which can be written to only once.
- [OnceRef](https://docs.rs/struct.OnceRef.html)
- A thread-safe cell which can be written to only once.

# once_cell - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/latest/once_cell/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, [ unsync::OnceCell](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.OnceCell.html) and

[. A](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.OnceCell.html)

`sync::OnceCell``OnceCell` might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can
be assigned to at most once and provides direct access to the stored
contents. The core API looks *roughly*like this (and there’s much more inside, read on!):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T> OnceCell<T> {
    const fn new() -> OnceCell<T> { ... }
    fn set(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T> { ... }
    fn get(&self) -> Option<&T> { ... }
}
```
Note that, like with [ RefCell](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html) and

[, the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex``set` method requires
only a shared reference. Because of the single assignment restriction `get`
can return a `&T` instead of `Ref<T>` or `MutexGuard<T>`.The `sync` flavor is thread-safe (that is, implements the [ Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Sync.html) trait),
while the

`unsync` one is not.[§](https://docs.rs#recipes)Recipes

`OnceCell` might be useful for a variety of patterns.

[§](https://docs.rs#safe-initialization-of-global-data)Safe Initialization of Global Data

```
use std::{env, io};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Logger {
    // ...
}
static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Logger> = OnceCell::new();
impl Logger {
    pub fn global() -> &'static Logger {
        INSTANCE.get().expect("logger is not initialized")
    }
    fn from_cli(args: env::Args) -> Result<Logger, std::io::Error> {
       // ...
    }
}
fn main() {
    let logger = Logger::from_cli(env::args()).unwrap();
    INSTANCE.set(logger).unwrap();
    // use `Logger::global()` from now on
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazy-initialized-global-data)Lazy Initialized Global Data

This is essentially the `lazy_static!` macro, but without a macro.

```
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
fn global_data() -> &'static Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>> {
    static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = OnceCell::new();
    INSTANCE.get_or_init(|| {
        let mut m = HashMap::new();
        m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
        m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
        Mutex::new(m)
    })
}
```
There are also the [ sync::Lazy](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.Lazy.html) and

[convenience types to streamline this pattern:](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.Lazy.html)

`unsync::Lazy````
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA: Lazy<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = Lazy::new(|| {
    let mut m = HashMap::new();
    m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
    m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
    Mutex::new(m)
});
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", GLOBAL_DATA.lock().unwrap());
}
```
Note that the variable that holds `Lazy` is declared as `static`, *not*
`const`. This is important: using `const` instead compiles, but works wrong.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-purpose-lazy-evaluation)General purpose lazy evaluation

Unlike `lazy_static!`, `Lazy` works with local variables.

```
use once_cell::unsync::Lazy;
fn main() {
    let ctx = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let thunk = Lazy::new(|| {
        ctx.iter().sum::<i32>()
    });
    assert_eq!(*thunk, 6);
}
```
If you need a lazy field in a struct, you probably should use `OnceCell`
directly, because that will allow you to access `self` during
initialization.

```
use std::{fs, path::PathBuf};
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
struct Ctx {
    config_path: PathBuf,
    config: OnceCell<String>,
}
impl Ctx {
    pub fn get_config(&self) -> Result<&str, std::io::Error> {
        let cfg = self.config.get_or_try_init(|| {
            fs::read_to_string(&self.config_path)
        })?;
        Ok(cfg.as_str())
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazily-compiled-regex)Lazily Compiled Regex

This is a `regex!` macro which takes a string literal and returns an
*expression* that evaluates to a `&'static Regex`:

```
macro_rules! regex {
    ($re:literal $(,)?) => {{
        static RE: once_cell::sync::OnceCell<regex::Regex> = once_cell::sync::OnceCell::new();
        RE.get_or_init(|| regex::Regex::new($re).unwrap())
    }};
}
```
This macro can be useful to avoid the “compile regex on every loop iteration” problem.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-include_bytes)Runtime `include_bytes!`

The `include_bytes` macro is useful to include test resources, but it slows
down test compilation a lot. An alternative is to load the resources at
runtime:

```
use std::path::Path;
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct TestResource {
    path: &'static str,
    cell: OnceCell<Vec<u8>>,
}
impl TestResource {
    pub const fn new(path: &'static str) -> TestResource {
        TestResource { path, cell: OnceCell::new() }
    }
    pub fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        self.cell.get_or_init(|| {
            let dir = std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR").unwrap();
            let path = Path::new(dir.as_str()).join(self.path);
            std::fs::read(&path).unwrap_or_else(|_err| {
                panic!("failed to load test resource: {}", path.display())
            })
        }).as_slice()
    }
}
static TEST_IMAGE: TestResource = TestResource::new("test_data/lena.png");
#[test]
fn test_sobel_filter() {
    let rgb: &[u8] = TEST_IMAGE.bytes();
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lateinit)`lateinit`

`LateInit` type for delayed initialization. It is reminiscent of Kotlin’s
`lateinit` keyword and allows construction of cyclic data structures:

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct LateInit<T> { cell: OnceCell<T> }
impl<T> LateInit<T> {
    pub fn init(&self, value: T) {
        assert!(self.cell.set(value).is_ok())
    }
}
impl<T> Default for LateInit<T> {
    fn default() -> Self { LateInit { cell: OnceCell::default() } }
}
impl<T> std::ops::Deref for LateInit<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        self.cell.get().unwrap()
    }
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct A<'a> {
    b: LateInit<&'a B<'a>>,
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct B<'a> {
    a: LateInit<&'a A<'a>>
}
fn build_cycle() {
    let a = A::default();
    let b = B::default();
    a.b.init(&b);
    b.a.init(&a);
    let _a = &a.b.a.b.a;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-with-std)Comparison with std

| `!Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `Cell<T>` | `T` | requires `T: Copy`for`get` |
| `RefCell<T>` | `RefMut<T>`/`Ref<T>` | may panic at runtime |
| `unsync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once |

| `Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `AtomicT` | `T` | works only with certain `Copy`types |
| `Mutex<T>` | `MutexGuard<T>` | may deadlock at runtime, may block the thread |
| `sync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once, may block the thread |

Technically, calling `get_or_init` will also cause a panic or a deadlock if
it recursively calls itself. However, because the assignment can happen only
once, such cases should be more rare than equivalents with `RefCell` and
`Mutex`.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rustc-version)Minimum Supported `rustc` Version

If only the `std`, `alloc`, or `race` features are enabled, MSRV will be
updated conservatively, supporting at least latest 8 versions of the compiler.
When using other features, like `parking_lot`, MSRV might be updated more
frequently, up to the latest stable. In both cases, increasing MSRV is *not*
considered a semver-breaking change and requires only a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

The implementation is based on the
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/) and

[crates and](https://github.com/indiv0/lazycell/)

`lazy_cell`[. In some sense,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Once.html)

`std::sync::Once``once_cell` just streamlines and unifies
those APIs.To implement a sync flavor of `OnceCell`, this crates uses either a custom
re-implementation of `std::sync::Once` or `parking_lot::Mutex`. This is
controlled by the `parking_lot` feature (disabled by default). Performance
is the same for both cases, but the `parking_lot` based `OnceCell<T>` is
smaller by up to 16 bytes.

This crate uses `unsafe`.

[§](https://docs.rs#faq)F.A.Q.

**Should I use the sync or unsync flavor?**

Because Rust compiler checks thread safety for you, it’s impossible to
accidentally use `unsync` where `sync` is required. So, use `unsync` in
single-threaded code and `sync` in multi-threaded. It’s easy to switch
between the two if code becomes multi-threaded later.

At the moment, `unsync` has an additional benefit that reentrant
initialization causes a panic, which might be easier to debug than a
deadlock.

**Does this crate support async?**

No, but you can use
[ async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell) instead.

**Does this crate support  no_std?**

Yes, but with caveats. `OnceCell` is a synchronization primitive which
*semantically* relies on blocking. `OnceCell` guarantees that at most one
`f` will be called to compute the value. If two threads of execution call
`get_or_init` concurrently, one of them has to wait.

Waiting fundamentally requires OS support. Execution environment needs to
understand who waits on whom to prevent deadlocks due to priority inversion.
You *could* make code to compile by blindly using pure spinlocks, but the
runtime behavior would be subtly wrong.

Given these constraints, `once_cell` provides the following options:

- The `race`module provides similar, but distinct synchronization primitive which is compatible with`no_std`. With`race`, the`f`function can be called multiple times by different threads, but only one thread will win to install the value.
- `critical-section`feature (with a- `-`, not- `_`) uses- `critical_section`to implement blocking.

**Can I bring my own mutex?**

There is [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell) to
allow just that.

**Should I use  std::cell::OnceCell, once_cell, or lazy_static?**

If you can use `std` version (your MSRV is at least 1.70, and you don’t need
extra features `once_cell` provides), use `std`. Otherwise, use `once_cell`.
Don’t use `lazy_static`.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related crates

- Most of this crate’s functionality is available in `std`starting with Rust 1.70. See`std::cell::OnceCell`and`std::sync::OnceLock`.
- [double-checked-cell](https://github.com/niklasf/double-checked-cell)
- [lazy-init](https://crates.io/crates/lazy-init)
- [lazycell](https://crates.io/crates/lazycell)
- [mitochondria](https://crates.io/crates/mitochondria)
- [lazy_static](https://crates.io/crates/lazy_static)
- [async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell)
- [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell)(bring your own mutex)

# critical-section 1.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/critical-section/^1.1.3

# critical-section

This project is developed and maintained by the [HAL team](https://github.com/rust-embedded/wg#the-hal-team).

A critical section that works everywhere!

When writing software for embedded systems, it's common to use a "critical section"
as a basic primitive to control concurrency. A critical section is essentially a
mutex global to the whole process, that can be acquired by only one thread at a time.
This can be used to protect data behind mutexes, to [emulate atomics](https://crates.io/crates/portable-atomic) in
targets that don't support them, etc.

There's a wide range of possible implementations depending on the execution environment:

- For bare-metal single core, disabling interrupts in the current (only) core.
- For bare-metal multicore, disabling interrupts in the current core and acquiring a hardware spinlock to prevent other cores from entering a critical section concurrently.
- For bare-metal using a RTOS, using library functions for acquiring a critical section, often named "scheduler lock" or "kernel lock".
- For bare-metal running in non-privileged mode, calling some system call is usually needed.
- For `std`targets, acquiring a global`std::sync::Mutex`.

Libraries often need to use critical sections, but there's no universal API for this in `core`. This leads
library authors to hard-code them for their target, or at best add some `cfg`s to support a few targets.
This doesn't scale since there are many targets out there, and in the general case it's impossible to know
which critical section implementation is needed from the Rust target alone. For example, the `thumbv7em-none-eabi` target
could be cases 1-4 from the above list.

This crate solves the problem by providing this missing universal API.

- It provides functions `acquire`,`release`and`with`that libraries can directly use.
- It provides a way for any crate to supply an implementation. This allows "target support" crates such as architecture crates (`cortex-m`,`riscv`), RTOS bindings, or HALs for multicore chips to supply the correct implementation so that all the crates in the dependency tree automatically use it.

## Usage in `no-std` binaries.

First, add a dependency on a crate providing a critical section implementation. Enable the `critical-section-*` Cargo feature if required by the crate.

Implementations are typically provided by either architecture-support crates, HAL crates, and OS/RTOS bindings, including:

- The `cortex-m``critical-section-single-core`feature
- The `riscv``critical-section-single-hart`feature
- The `msp430``critical-section-single-core`feature
- The `rp2040-hal``critical-section-impl`feature
- The `avr-device``critical-section-impl`feature
- The `esp-hal-common`
- The `embassy-rp``critical-section-impl`feature
- The `nrf-softdevice``critical-section-impl`feature

For example, for single-core Cortex-M targets, you can use:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.7.6",  = ["critical-section-single-core"]}
```
Then you can use `critical_section::with()`.

```
use Cell;
use Mutex;
static MY_VALUE:  = new;
with;
#  // needed for `cargo test --features std`
#
```
## Usage in `std` binaries.

Add the `critical-section` dependency to `Cargo.toml` enabling the `std` feature. This makes the `critical-section` crate itself
provide an implementation based on `std::sync::Mutex`, so you don't have to add any other dependency.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.1",  = ["std"]}
```
## Usage in libraries

If you're writing a library intended to be portable across many targets, simply add a dependency on `critical-section`
and use `critical_section::free` and/or `Mutex` as usual.

**Do not** add any dependency supplying a critical section implementation. Do not enable any `critical-section-*` Cargo feature.
This has to be done by the end user, enabling the correct implementation for their target.

**Do not** enable any Cargo feature in `critical-section`.

## Usage in `std` tests for `no-std` libraries.

If you want to run `std`-using tests in otherwise `no-std` libraries, enable the `std` feature in `dev-dependencies` only.
This way the main target will use the `no-std` implementation chosen by the end-user's binary, and only the test targets
will use the `std` implementation.

```
[]
 = "1.1"
[]
 = {  = "1.1",  = ["std"]}
```
## Providing an implementation

Crates adding support for a particular architecture, chip or operating system should provide a critical section implementation.
It is **strongly recommended** to gate the implementation behind a feature, so the user can still use another implementation
if needed (having two implementations in the same binary will cause linking to fail).

Add the dependency, and a `critical-section-*` feature to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
# Enable critical section implementation that does "foo"
 = ["critical-section/restore-state-bool"]
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = true }
```
Then, provide the critical implementation like this:

```
#  // needed for `cargo test --features std`
#
```
## Troubleshooting

### Undefined reference errors

If you get an error like these:

```
undefined reference to `_critical_section_1_0_acquire'
undefined reference to `_critical_section_1_0_release'
```
it is because you (or a library) are using `critical_section::with` without providing a critical section implementation.
Make sure you're depending on a crate providing the implementation, and have enabled the `critical-section-*` feature in it if required. See the `Usage` section above.

The error can also be caused by having the dependency but never `use`ing it. This can be fixed by adding a dummy `use`:

```
use the_cs_impl_crate as _;
```
### Duplicate symbol errors

If you get errors like these:

```
error: symbol `_critical_section_1_0_acquire` is already defined
```
it is because you have two crates trying to provide a critical section implementation. You can only have one implementation in a program.

You can use `cargo tree --format '{p} {f}'` to view all dependencies and their enabled features. Make sure
that in the whole dependency tree, exactly one implementation is provided.

Check for multiple versions of the same crate as well. For example, check the `critical-section-single-core`
feature is not enabled for both `cortex-m` 0.7 and 0.8.

## Why not generics?

An alternative solution would be to use a `CriticalSection` trait, and make all
code that needs acquiring the critical section generic over it. This has a few problems:

- It would require passing it as a generic param to a very big amount of code, which would be quite unergonomic.
- It's common to put `Mutex`es in`static`variables, and`static`s can't be generic.
- It would allow mixing different critical section implementations in the same program, which would be unsound.

## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on the following Rust versions:

- If the `std`feature is not enabled: stable Rust 1.54 and up.
- If the `std`feature is enabled: stable Rust 1.63 and up.

It might compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

See [here](https://docs.rs/docs/msrv.md) for details on how the MSRV may be upgraded.

# parking_lot_core 0.9.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/parking_lot_core/^0.9.10

This library exposes a low-level API for creating your own efficient synchronization primitives.

# The parking lot

To keep synchronization primitives small, all thread queuing and suspending
functionality is offloaded to the *parking lot*. The idea behind this is based
on the Webkit [ WTF::ParkingLot](https://webkit.org/blog/6161/locking-in-webkit/)
class, which essentially consists of a hash table mapping of lock addresses
to queues of parked (sleeping) threads. The Webkit parking lot was itself
inspired by Linux

[futexes](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/futex.2.html), but it is more powerful since it allows invoking callbacks while holding a queue lock.

There are two main operations that can be performed on the parking lot:

- *Parking*refers to suspending the thread while simultaneously enqueuing it on a queue keyed by some address.
- *Unparking*refers to dequeuing a thread from a queue keyed by some address and resuming it.

See the documentation of the individual functions for more details.

# Building custom synchronization primitives

Building custom synchronization primitives is very simple since the parking
lot takes care of all the hard parts for you. A simple example for a
custom primitive would be to integrate a `Mutex` inside another data type.
Since a mutex only requires 2 bits, it can share space with other data.
For example, one could create an `ArcMutex` type that combines the atomic
reference count and the two mutex bits in the same atomic word.

# portable-atomic 1.13.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/portable-atomic/^1.8

# portable-atomic

Portable atomic types including support for 128-bit atomics, atomic float, etc.

- Provide all atomic integer types (`Atomic{I,U}{8,16,32,64}`) for all targets that can use atomic CAS. (i.e., all targets that can use`std`, and most no-std targets)
- Provide `AtomicI128`and`AtomicU128`.
- Provide `AtomicF32`and`AtomicF64`. ([optional, requires the](https://docs.rs#optional-features-float))`float`feature
- Provide `AtomicF16`and`AtomicF128`for[unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/116909). (`f16`and`f128`[optional, requires the](https://docs.rs#optional-features-float))`float`feature and unstable cfgs
- Provide atomic load/store for targets where atomic is not available at all in the standard library. (RISC-V without A-extension, MSP430, AVR)
- Provide atomic CAS for targets where atomic CAS is not available in the standard library. (thumbv6m, pre-v6 Arm, RISC-V without A-extension, MSP430, AVR, Xtensa, etc.) (always enabled for MSP430 and AVR, [optional](https://docs.rs#optional-features-critical-section)otherwise)
- Make features that require newer compilers, such as `fetch_{max,min}``fetch_update``as_ptr``from_ptr``AtomicBool::fetch_not``AtomicPtr::fetch_*`[stronger CAS failure ordering](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/98383)available on Rust 1.34+.
- Provide workaround for bugs in the standard library's atomic-related APIs, such as [rust-lang/rust#100650](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/100650),`fence`/`compiler_fence`on MSP430 that cause LLVM error, etc.

portable-atomic version of `std::sync::Arc` is provided by the [portable-atomic-util](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/tree/HEAD/portable-atomic-util) crate.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "1"
```
The default features are mainly for users who use atomics larger than the pointer width. If you don't need them, disabling the default features may reduce code size and compile time slightly.

```
[]
 = {  = "1",  = false }
```
If your crate supports no-std environment and requires atomic CAS, enabling the `require-cas` feature will allow the portable-atomic to display a [helpful error message](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/pull/100) to users on targets requiring additional action on the user side to provide atomic CAS.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.3",  = false,  = ["require-cas"] }
```
(Since 1.8, portable-atomic can display a [helpful error message](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/pull/181) even without the `require-cas` feature when the rustc version is 1.78+. However, the `require-cas` feature also allows rejecting builds at an earlier stage, we recommend enabling it unless enabling it causes [problems](https://github.com/matklad/once_cell/pull/267).)

## 128-bit atomics support

Native 128-bit atomic operations are available on x86_64 (Rust 1.59+), AArch64 (Rust 1.59+), riscv64 (Rust 1.59+), Arm64EC (Rust 1.84+), s390x (Rust 1.84+), and powerpc64 (Rust 1.95+), otherwise the fallback implementation is used.

On x86_64, even if `cmpxchg16b` is not available at compile-time (Note: `cmpxchg16b` target feature is enabled by default only on Apple, Windows (except Windows 7), and Fuchsia targets), run-time detection checks whether `cmpxchg16b` is available. If `cmpxchg16b` is not available at either compile-time or run-time detection, the fallback implementation is used. See also [ portable_atomic_no_outline_atomics](https://docs.rs#optional-cfg-no-outline-atomics) cfg.

They are usually implemented using inline assembly, and when using Miri or ThreadSanitizer that do not support inline assembly, core intrinsics are used instead of inline assembly if possible.

See the [ atomic128 module's readme](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/blob/HEAD/src/imp/atomic128/README.md) for details.

## Optional features/cfgs

portable-atomic provides features and cfgs to allow enabling specific APIs and customizing its behavior.

Some options have both a feature and a cfg. When both exist, it indicates that the feature does not follow Cargo's recommendation that [features should be additive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/cargo/reference/features.html#feature-unification). Therefore, the maintainer's recommendation is to use cfg instead of feature. However, in the embedded ecosystem, it is very common to use features in such places, so these options provide both so you can choose based on your preference.

One of the ways to enable cfg is to set [rustflags in the cargo config](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#targettriplerustflags):

```
# .cargo/config.toml
[<target>]
 = ["--cfg", "portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_single_core"]
```
Or set environment variable:

```
RUSTFLAGS="--cfg portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_single_core"
```
-
`fallback`feature*(enabled by default)*Enable fallback implementations.This enables atomic types with larger than the width supported by atomic instructions available on the current target. If the current target [supports 128-bit atomics](https://docs.rs#128-bit-atomics-support), this is no-op.This uses fallback implementation that using global locks by default. The following features/cfgs change this behavior: - `unsafe-assume-single-core`feature /- `portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_single_core`cfg- If your target is single-core and calling interrupt disable instructions is safe, this is a safer and more efficient option.

- `unsafe-assume-privileged`feature /- `portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_privileged`cfg- If your target is multi-core and calling interrupt disable instructions is safe, this is a safer option.

-
`float`feature`AtomicF{32,64}`.If you want atomic types for unstable float types ( `f16`and`f128``portable_atomic_unstable_f16`cfg for`AtomicF16`,`portable_atomic_unstable_f128`cfg for`AtomicF128`,[there is no possibility that both feature and cfg will be provided for unstable options.](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/pull/200#issuecomment-2682252991)).

[!NOTE]

- Atomic float's
`fetch_{add,sub,min,max}`are usually implemented using CAS loops, which can be slower than equivalent operations of atomic integers. As an exception, AArch64 with FEAT_LSFE and GPU targets have atomic float instructions and we use them on AArch64 when`lsfe`target feature is available at compile-time. We[plan to use atomic float instructions for GPU targets as well in the future.](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/issues/34)- Unstable cfgs are outside of the normal semver guarantees and minor or patch versions of portable-atomic may make breaking changes to them at any time.

-
`std`feature`std`.
-
`require-cas`feature[Usage](https://docs.rs#usage)section for usage of this feature.
-
`serde`feature`serde::{Serialize,Deserialize}`for atomic types.Note: - The MSRV when this feature is enabled depends on the MSRV of [serde](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde).

- The MSRV when this feature is enabled depends on the MSRV of
-
`critical-section`feature[critical-section](https://github.com/rust-embedded/critical-section)to provide atomic CAS for targets where atomic CAS is not available in the standard library.`critical-section`support is useful to get atomic CAS when the`unsafe-assume-single-core`feature (or`portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_single_core`cfg)

[!NOTE]

When enabling this feature, you should provide a suitable critical section implementation for the current target, see the

[critical-section](https://github.com/rust-embedded/critical-section)documentation for details on how to do so.
With this feature, critical sections are taken for all atomic operations, while with

`unsafe-assume-single-core`feature[some operations](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/blob/HEAD/src/imp/interrupt/README.md#no-disable-interrupts)don't require disabling interrupts. Therefore, for better performance, if all the`critical-section`implementation for your target does is disable interrupts, prefer using`unsafe-assume-single-core`feature (or`portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_single_core`cfg) instead.
It is usually

discouragedto always enable this feature in libraries that depend on`portable-atomic`.Enabling this feature will prevent the end user from having the chance to take advantage of other (potentially) efficient implementations (implementations provided by

`unsafe-assume-single-core`feature mentioned above, implementation proposed in[#60](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/issues/60), etc.). Also, targets that are currently unsupported may be supported in the future.The recommended approach for libraries is to leave it up to the end user whether or not to enable this feature. (However, it may make sense to enable this feature by default for libraries specific to a platform where other implementations are known not to work.)

As an example, the end-user's

`Cargo.toml`that uses a crate that provides a critical-section implementation and a crate that depends on portable-atomic as an option would be expected to look like this:`[] = { = "1", = false, = ["critical-section"] } = "..." = { = "...", = ["portable-atomic"] }`
Enabling both this feature and

`unsafe-assume-single-core`feature (or`portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_single_core`cfg) will result in a compile error.
Enabling both this feature and

`unsafe-assume-privileged`feature (or`portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_privileged`cfg) will result in a compile error.
The MSRV when this feature is enabled depends on the MSRV of

[critical-section](https://github.com/rust-embedded/critical-section).

-
`unsafe-assume-single-core`feature /`portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_single_core`cfg- When this feature/cfg is enabled, this crate provides atomic CAS for targets where atomic CAS is not available in the standard library by disabling interrupts.
- When both this feature/cfg and enabled-by-default `fallback`feature is enabled, this crate provides atomic types with larger than the width supported by native instructions by disabling interrupts.

[!WARNING] This feature/cfg is

`unsafe`, and note the following safety requirements:

Enabling this feature/cfg for multi-core systems is always

unsound.
This uses privileged instructions to disable interrupts, so it usually doesn't work on unprivileged mode.

Enabling this feature/cfg in an environment where privileged instructions are not available, or if the instructions used are not sufficient to disable interrupts in the system, it is also usually considered

unsound, although the details are system-dependent.The following are known cases:

- On Arm (except for M-Profile architectures), this disables only IRQs by default. For many systems (e.g., GBA) this is enough. If the system need to disable both IRQs and FIQs, you need to enable the
`disable-fiq`feature (or`portable_atomic_disable_fiq`cfg) together.- On RISC-V, this generates code for machine-mode (M-mode) by default. If you enable the
`s-mode`feature (or`portable_atomic_s_mode`cfg) together, this generates code for supervisor-mode (S-mode). In particular,`qemu-system-riscv*`uses[OpenSBI](https://github.com/riscv-software-src/opensbi)as the default firmware.

Consider using the [ unsafe-assume-privileged feature (or portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_privileged cfg)](https://docs.rs#optional-features-unsafe-assume-privileged) for multi-core systems with atomic CAS.

Consider using the [ critical-section feature](https://docs.rs#optional-features-critical-section) for systems that cannot use this feature/cfg.

See also the [ interrupt module's readme](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/blob/HEAD/src/imp/interrupt/README.md).

[!NOTE]

It is

very strongly discouragedto enable this feature/cfg in libraries that depend on`portable-atomic`.The recommended approach for libraries is to leave it up to the end user whether or not to enable this feature/cfg. (However, it may make sense to enable this feature/cfg by default for libraries specific to a platform where it is guaranteed to always be sound, for example in a hardware abstraction layer targeting a single-core chip.)

Enabling this feature/cfg for unsupported architectures will result in a compile error.

- Arm, RISC-V, and Xtensa are currently supported. (Since all MSP430 and AVR are single-core, we always provide atomic CAS for them without this feature/cfg.)
- Feel free to
[submit an issue](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/issues/new)if your target is not supported yet.
Enabling this feature/cfg for targets where privileged instructions are obviously unavailable (e.g., Linux) will result in a compile error.

- Feel free to
[submit an issue](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/issues/new)if your target supports privileged instructions but the build rejected.
Enabling both this feature/cfg and

`critical-section`feature will result in a compile error.
When both this feature/cfg and

`unsafe-assume-privileged`feature (or`portable_atomic_unsafe_assume_privileged`cfg) are enabled, this feature/cfg is preferred.

-

- When both this feature/cfg and enabled-by-default
